waypoints.name: Stuart Lake Trailhead (FR 7601)
waypoints.directions: From US 2 at the west edge of Leavenworth, turn onto Icicle Creek Road and drive about 8.4 miles, then turn left onto FR 7601 and follow the bumpy gravel road about 3.7 miles to the Stuart Lake Trailhead at its end. FR 7601 is normally closed in winter. A Northwest Forest Pass is required, and a day-use Enchantment permit is self-issued at the trailhead.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Lake (outlet, north end) — camp and last water
waypoints.directions: Take the trail up Mountaineer Creek, crossing it on a log bridge at about 1.5 miles, and leave the Lake Stuart Trail at its junction around 2.25 miles for the Colchuck Lake Trail. It climbs steeply, finishing over boulders and moraine to the north end of Colchuck Lake, about 4 miles and 2,280 ft from the car. Fill water here.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Balanced Rock summit
waypoints.directions: Follow the trail around the lake onto the cairned Aasgard Pass climbers' trail and climb talus and heather to about 400 ft above the lake, then break left through dense brush to the base gully below the wall. The route starts with Let It Burn on the wall's lower left, reached over loose 3rd and 4th class rock, and about ten pitches finish up the West Face to the summit.

removed.wp: Colchuck Lake (outlet, north end) — camp and last water

waypoints.name: Rachel Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Trail #1313 start off FR 4930; Northwest Forest Pass plus self-issued wilderness permit required (USFS Rachel Lake Trailhead page).
waypoints.directions: From I-90 Exit 62, follow Kachess Lake Road to FS Road 4930 and drive it to the road end at about 2,800 ft. Trail #1313 leaves the parking area; a Northwest Forest Pass plus a self-issued wilderness permit are required at the board.

waypoints.name: Rachel Lake
waypoints.note: ~4.1 mi from the trailhead, at the top of the steep, rooty 'mile from hell' climb.
waypoints.directions: Trail #1313 runs beside Box Canyon Creek on gentle grade for roughly 2.75 miles, crossing several side streams and cascades — water is reliable the whole way, so there is no need to carry much from the car. Past the creek crossing the trail turns into the rooty, rocky boot-beaten climb locals call the 'mile from hell': about 1,300 ft of gain in a mile with large step-ups and no switchbacks. It is a fitness crux, not a technical one, but it is brutal under a full pack.

waypoints.name: Rampart Ridge / Rampart Lakes junction
waypoints.note: Ridge crest above Rachel Lake where the maintained trail splits toward Rampart Lakes and Lila Lake.
waypoints.directions: At the lake a use path branches off near the outhouse and skirts the north shore. From there it switchbacks steeply up rocky tread for about half a mile to the crest of Rampart Ridge, where the maintained trail splits toward Rampart Lakes and toward Lila Lake.

waypoints.name: Alta climbers' path turnoff (cairn)
waypoints.note: Cairned fork on the Lila Lake trail about 0.3 mi past the Rampart Ridge junction, where the unmarked climbers' path up Alta's south ridge leaves on the left.
waypoints.directions: At the ridge-top junction above Rachel Lake, go right toward Lila Lake (the left branch leads to Rampart Lakes). The tread is brushy in places but always clear; after about 0.3 mile a cairn marks the fork where the Lila Lake trail carries straight on and the climbers' path to Alta leaves on the left.

waypoints.name: Alta Mountain summit
waypoints.note: Reached past several false summits along the exposed ridge crest.
waypoints.directions: At the cairned fork on the Lila Lake trail an unmarked climbers' path leaves the maintained trail and follows the ridge crest toward the summit block. It starts steep, loose and shadeless with large steps, then eases onto a narrow crest with sustained exposure: expect several class 2-3 moves, at least one near-vertical step of six to eight feet with good holds, a short class 3 downclimb near the top, and three or more false summits before the real one. Do not attempt this stretch with snow on the crest or on wet rock — the path skirts a cliff edge and the fall consequences are serious. Helmets are worth wearing for the loose rock.

waypoints.name: Andrews Creek Trailhead
waypoints.directions: From Highway 20 in Winthrop, turn onto County Road 1213 (West Chewuch Road) and follow it about 6 miles to where it joins Forest Road 51. Continue north on FR 51 to the end of the pavement and turn right into the Andrews Creek Trailhead at 3,050 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is needed to park, and a free self-issued Pasayten Wilderness permit is required.

waypoints.name: Cathedral Pass (foot of the North Ridge)
waypoints.directions: Hike Andrews Creek Trail #504 about 12 miles over Andrews Pass, then 3 miles down to the Spanish Camp guard station, and take the trail on the right just before the cabin 3 miles to Upper Cathedral Lake. Continue on the trail up to Cathedral Pass, the saddle between Amphitheater Mountain and Cathedral Peak; the North Ridge rises straight south from the pass.

waypoints.name: Amphitheater Mountain summit
waypoints.directions: Scramble up the ridge from the pass to where roping up is worthwhile, then follow the blunt crest south through several short steep steps of up to 5.5 to the summit plateau.

removed.wp: Cathedral Pass (foot of the North Ridge)

waypoints.name: Maynard Burn (Tyler Peak) Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR 2870-120 off Palo Alto Rd; Northwest Forest Pass required to park here.
waypoints.directions: Drive FR 2870 off Palo Alto Road to its end at the signed Baldy/Tyler Peak trailhead, a gravel pullout for about a dozen cars in the Upper Dungeness drainage of the Hood Canal Ranger District.

waypoints.name: Mueller Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Rock-hop crossing just past the trailhead; the rocks here are slick.
waypoints.directions: Follow the old roadbed a short distance from the lot; at about 0.3 mile the Baldy climbers' path (Lower Maynard Burn Trail #816) splits off to the right and begins climbing in earnest, and at roughly half a mile it crosses a decommissioned logging road. Mueller Creek parallels these early switchbacks and is the last dependable water low on the mountain — top off here, especially late in the summer; the only water higher up is a small stream off a steep side path near the ridge crest.

waypoints.name: Maynard Burn fire-line clearing
waypoints.note: Flat clearing where the trail crosses an old decommissioned road/fire barrier; used as a camp before the steep push.
waypoints.directions: Steep switchbacks gain roughly 1,600 ft in under a mile. At about 1.3 miles the path crosses the old Maynard Burn track near a short junction with the Upper Dungeness Trail (#833.2), and continues above it as the Upper Maynard Burn Trail (#816.2).

waypoints.name: Eroded ravine section
waypoints.note: Steepest stretch of the climb -- crumbly, narrow (barely one-foot-wide) tread across a rocky ravine; the ~3,000 ft gain in the first 2 miles ends here.
waypoints.directions: This is the relentless section: narrow tread, in places barely a foot wide, sidehilling an eroding slope on loose dirt and gravel, with crumbly footing where it crosses the rocky ravine. By about two miles the forest thins and Tyler Peak comes into view.

waypoints.name: Ridge crest water source
waypoints.note: Trail tops out on the ridge crest; the last water on the route is a small meadow stream down a short, steep side path here, with none beyond; exposed to frequent wind blasts.
waypoints.directions: Above the ravine the tread turns faint and muddy through boggy meadow benches where flagging and cairns are sparse, then breaks out onto the open ridge crest east of Baldy at roughly 2.7 miles. This is where the route leaves the trees for good and the first views north to the Strait of Juan de Fuca and Vancouver Island open up — fix the spot in your memory, because it is the key handrail on the way down in fog.

waypoints.name: Gray Wolf Ridge saddle
waypoints.note: Low point where the Baldy climbers' path joins Gray Wolf Ridge proper; Class 1-2 talus/ridge walking begins here.
waypoints.directions: A short step west along the crest ends the formal trail tread. Everything above is cross-country over talus and heather with no maintained path, fully exposed to wind and cloud.

waypoints.name: False summit (Pt. 6537)
waypoints.note: Marked as a separate high point on USGS maps -- the path climbs over its top before continuing west along the ridge.
waypoints.directions: Continue west along the open crest on talus. In poor visibility this bump is routinely mistaken for the true top, and it is the spot people most often lose the line on the descent, so note how you pass it on the way up.

waypoints.name: Baldy summit
waypoints.note: True summit; 360-degree views of Mount Constance, the Strait of Juan de Fuca, and Vancouver Island.
waypoints.directions: A final few hundred feet of open ridge west from the bump reaches the true summit, which holds an old campsite. Lingering snow can bury the boot path through this section into June and the crest catches the full wind; carry a map or GPS track, since this is the stretch that causes trouble when cloud rolls in.

waypoints.name: Holden Village / Railroad Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Access via Lady of the Lake ferry to Lucerne then the Holden Village shuttle bus; standard-route parties stage here.
waypoints.directions: There is no road in. Take the Lake Chelan ferry from Chelan or Field's Point to Lucerne, then the village shuttle up from the landing. Plan the whole trip around the boat and bus timetable in both directions — parties who miss the connection out spend an extra night at the village.

waypoints.name: Railroad Creek Trail / Holden Lake Trail junction
waypoints.note: Leave the valley-bottom trail here and climb toward Holden Lake on dry, open-pine switchbacks.
waypoints.directions: Walk the gravel road and Railroad Creek Trail (FST 1256) west out of the village for about a mile. The Holden Lake Trail leaves it on the right and is signed.

waypoints.name: Holden Lake
waypoints.note: Common base camp in a glacial basin directly below the Mary Green Glacier; water is scarce on the approach so fill up here.
waypoints.directions: Steady climbing for several miles through forest and brush, with a few small side creeks that run reliably. Black flies are thick through the lower part of this stretch. The trail ends in the cirque directly under Bonanza's east face.

waypoints.name: Holden Pass high camp
waypoints.note: Alternate, higher camp that most summit parties use to shorten summit day; some brushy bushwhacking to reach it.
waypoints.directions: From the lake outlet the tread fades out. Skirt the north shore through slide alder and talus — genuine bushwhacking and route-finding, worse early season when the water is high — then climb a hillside traverse northwest to the pass.

waypoints.name: Mary Green Glacier, north edge
waypoints.note: Rising traverse to a snowfield below slabs, then a scramble onto the glacier's north edge — rope up for the crossing here.
waypoints.directions: Rising traverse west from the pass along the ridge and slope to a snowfield beneath rock slabs at roughly 7,000 to 7,300 ft. Scramble the class 3 slabs above it, starting high and to the right to keep clear of a waterfall. The gullies here sit below a retreating glacier margin and are loose, so stay out of the fall line and out from under any party above you.

waypoints.name: Moat crossing, glacier's upper corner
waypoints.note: Cross the moat via a snow bridge onto rock; bridges can collapse by late season, sometimes forcing a detour right onto rock.
waypoints.directions: Bear west along the glacier's north (climber's right) edge, then traverse southwest under the base of Bonanza's northeast ridge to the glacier's upper corner. Finish up the steep snow finger to its high point and look for the exit onto rock; an overhanging snow lip can be as much of an obstacle as the moat itself. The crossing gets harder as the season goes on and can turn into a maze of crevasses rather than a single step across.

waypoints.name: Bonanza Peak summit
waypoints.note: True summit reached after the moat and a short Class 3-4 finish; descent reverses the route with about four rappels off fixed stations.
waypoints.directions: Off the snow, climb class 3-4 rock just right of a gully for several rope-lengths, then traverse left into a second gully and scramble to a notch on the northeast ridge just north of the top. From the notch follow the crest past a run of large blocks to the summit horn. The rock along here is loose and this is where the route's rockfall problem lives — anything knocked off funnels straight down the gullies onto whoever is below.

waypoints.name: Holden Village / Railroad Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Reached only by Lady of the Lake ferry from Chelan/Field's Point to Lucerne, then the Holden Village shuttle bus up FS Rd 8301; Railroad Creek Trail starts at the village.
waypoints.directions: There is no road in, and the whole trip is gated by the boat and bus timetable rather than by the weather window alone — build the itinerary around sailing days first. Boats leave from Chelan or Field's Point Landing for the Lucerne dock, and the village bus climbs the last few miles of FS Road 8301 from there.

waypoints.name: Railroad Creek Trail / Holden Lake Trail junction
waypoints.note: Trail forks here; leave the Railroad Creek/Hart-Lyman Lake Trail and turn onto the Holden Lake Trail toward the climbers' basin.
waypoints.directions: From the village, follow the Railroad Creek Trail (FST 1256) west up the valley for about a mile on easy, near-level grade to the signed fork.

waypoints.name: Holden Lake
waypoints.note: Glacial-basin lake camp with the first direct views of Bonanza Peak and the Mary Green Glacier; trail up is dry, south-facing switchbacks with little shade or water.
waypoints.directions: Turn right at the fork and climb roughly four miles and 1,700 ft of switchbacks up out of the valley to the lake basin. Carry water from the creek below rather than counting on finding any on the way up. The lake is the usual first-night camp, though it can be buggy.

waypoints.name: Holden Pass high camp
waypoints.note: Higher alternative camp above the lake that trims roughly 1,000 ft of gain off summit day; approach trail is well-defined but grown in with slide alder near the lake.
waypoints.directions: From the head of the lake, continue north-northwest on the climbers' path, gaining about 1,100 ft over heather benches and rocky terraces. This is effectively the last water on the route — everything above the pass has to be carried.

waypoints.name: Mary Green Glacier, north edge
waypoints.note: Rope up here before stepping onto the glacier; crevasses are usually easy to navigate but open up more by late summer.
waypoints.directions: From the pass, make a rising traverse west along the ridge over benches, talus and heather until a snowfield appears below a band of slabs. Scramble the slabs to reach the glacier's northern edge at about 7,800 ft. Expect loose footing and real route-finding on the benches; there is no single obvious line.

waypoints.name: Northeast Buttress base
waypoints.note: Branch off the glacier's climber's-right margin onto the buttress crest, about 3 hours from Holden Lake; start of the sustained 5.7 pitches.
waypoints.directions: Follow the glacier's climber's-right (north) margin west, then bend southwest along the foot of the northeast ridge to the glacier's upper southwest corner, where the buttress toe comes down to the ice. Holding the margin keeps crevasse exposure low but puts you under rock the whole way, so keep helmets on and keep moving. Most parties leave camp around first light so that this leg and the buttress above are climbed before the afternoon.

waypoints.name: Lichen-covered mid-buttress rock
waypoints.note: Mostly solid rock but shaded sections are slick with lichen where pitches step up to 5.8 — watch footing on traverses.
waypoints.directions: The crest steepens and narrows immediately above the toe. Several rope lengths of Class 4 and low fifth on and just right of the crest lead into the sustained section, where the climbing runs at 5.6-5.7 on and around the crest with wild exposure straight down to the glacier.

waypoints.name: Bonanza Peak summit
waypoints.note: Highest non-volcanic peak in Washington and the Chelan County highpoint; narrow, exposed summit block.
waypoints.directions: Above the licheny middle section the angle relents to easy fourth class along the crest, with gendarmes and notches to be turned or climbed over — watch rope drag through them. Figure roughly four hours on the ridge from the buttress base to the narrow, exposed true summit. Note that the descent does not reverse the buttress: it drops back onto the Mary Green Glacier and follows the standard route home to camp.

removed.wp: Railroad Creek Trail / Holden Lake Trail junction

waypoints.name: Trinity Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of Chiwawa River Road/FR-6200 (last 12 mi rough gravel); pay day-use fee or NW Forest Pass and self-issue a free Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the kiosk.
waypoints.directions: From US-2 at Coles Corner, take SR-207 north 4.2 miles past the Wenatchee River crossing and bear right onto Chiwawa Loop Road. After 1.3 miles turn left onto Chiwawa River Road (FS Road 62) and drive about 22 miles, the last 11 on rough gravel, keeping left at the final junction for the Trinity Trailhead at about 2,800 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required and a free wilderness permit is self-issued at the kiosk.

waypoints.name: Chiwawa River crossing
waypoints.note: Crossing of the Chiwawa River about three miles up the trail. There is no footbridge; cross on a log near the old bridge site, and expect to wade if the river is high.

waypoints.name: Buck Creek Pass
waypoints.note: Established camps in scattered trees and meadows; most parties base camp here for the climb, with a junction to the Flower Dome Trail #799 a half mile north.

waypoints.name: High Pass
waypoints.note: The old High Pass trail fades into talus and hard snow here. Contour through the pass and under Mount Berge, then climb a short Class 3 step onto the ridge just south of Point 7839.

waypoints.name: Louis Creek Basin camp
waypoints.note: Camp in the basin below Buck's southwest side, reached by an easy walk down from the faint saddle south of Point 7839. Stay high on the traverse from the Berge saddle to avoid waterfall slabs.

waypoints.name: Buck Mountain
waypoints.note: True summit; sweeping views of Glacier Peak, Clark Mountain, and the Napeequa valley — first climbed in 1948 by Carl Suback and Ray Rigg.

waypoints.name: SR-20 Pullout (Burgundy Col climbers' trail)
waypoints.directions: Park at the pullout on SR-20 near milepost 166, about three and three-quarters miles east of Washington Pass and directly across the valley from Silver Star Mountain. There's no numbered Forest Service trail here — this pullout is simply the start of an established but unofficial boot path used by climbers heading for Burgundy Col.

waypoints.name: Burgundy Creek bench camp — west side
Burgundy Col
waypoints.directions: Scramble down the loose talus embankment past the cairns into forest, pass the wilderness trail-register box, and cross Early Winters Creek on logs at about 4,080 ft — the logjam shifts year to year, so look up and down stream for the best one, and expect a cold, pushy ford in early season. The path winds through forest for about a quarter mile, then turns straight uphill between two small creeks and climbs relentlessly to the broad flat bench at ~6,460 ft (last reliable water); above the bench it climbs and traverses loose scree gullies and makes a rising traverse right beneath the cliffs on heather-covered slabs, with a final cairned stretch of very unstable scree over slab into the notch — do not take the obvious direct gully that appears to lead straight to the col, and travel tightly grouped, as this scree kicks rock onto anyone below.

waypoints.name: Burgundy Spire Summit
waypoints.directions: The route starts essentially straight off the col: the first pitch is directly above the notch and visually obvious, with no traverse along the base. Six to seven pitches lead up — 4th class with occasional mid-5th moves to a broad sandy ledge, along the ledge system toward the wide bowl, then the bowl's right side on loose exfoliating flakes to a tat-slung horn (the 5.8 crux, more rock quality than difficulty), past the horn to a hand crack in a flare and exposed 5.7–5.8 face climbing, then airy ridge with hand cracks, sharp arête moves and mandatory downclimbing to the heavily slung summit boulder.

waypoints.name: Alpental / Snow Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Self-serve day-use fee kiosk (Northwest Forest Pass or $5/day); trail departs the north end of the upper Alpental Ski Area parking lot.
waypoints.directions: From I-90 Exit 52 at Snoqualmie Pass, follow Alpental Road to its end, staying past the lower ski-area lots to the upper parking area.

waypoints.name: Source Lake Trail junction
waypoints.note: Leave the maintained Snow Lake Trail here on the unmaintained boot path toward Source Lake, a reliable water source in the Alpental Valley.
waypoints.directions: Pick up the valley trail and follow it up the South Fork Snoqualmie River — an old ski-area service road and cat track for the first half mile, then standard trail. It climbs gently through forest and avalanche-path brush for roughly a mile and a half with Chair Peak's north side in view ahead.

waypoints.name: Thumb Tack
waypoints.note: Prominent rock outcrop in the basin below Chair's east face; a common gear-cache and roping-up point before the final approach.
waypoints.directions: Cross the creek below Source Lake, which can be awkward at high flow, then climb the open slopes at the head of the valley and make a rising traverse into the cirque beneath Chair's east face. These slopes are the runouts below Chair, Snoqualmie Mountain and The Tooth, so move through them early and without stopping.

waypoints.name: North Face open-book base
waypoints.note: Left-facing open book in the center of the north face where the route begins; three pitches of 50-70 degree snow/ice.
waypoints.directions: From the outcrop head north and climb the gully toward the northeast ridge rather than taking the northeast slopes direct; this gully is a known avalanche path with a fatal history. Follow the ridge around onto the north face and traverse the talus and snow apron below it to the open book, which sits roughly halfway across the face. A moat can open at the base of the ice later in the season and complicate the last few metres.

waypoints.name: Col below summit block
waypoints.note: Small col reached after the ice pitches; a crux step up to roughly 80 degrees (occasionally bare 5.6 rock) leads to the summit from here.
waypoints.directions: Four pitches up the face. Ice bulges to about 70 degrees off the base, then two rope-lengths of sustained snow and easy mixed ground belayed off scrub trees, then a final steepening to the col. Stay on the centre line — the ground off to climber's right is thin and downsloping slab. The last belay sits close to the ridge crest, which is often corniced.

waypoints.name: Chair Peak summit
waypoints.note: Small summit block; the northeast side is heavily corniced in winter, stay toward the uncorniced center.
waypoints.directions: A short, steep step above the col — sometimes bare rock when the ice is thin — leads to roughly 20 feet of blocky scrambling, normally done unroped. Keep well off the northeast lip on the last moves.

waypoints.name: South-side gully rappels
waypoints.note: Descend via rappels down the gully on the south side of the east face; watch for parties and loose rock/ice falling from above.
waypoints.directions: Leave the summit over the false summit and head east down the standard descent gully to a notch in the southeast ridge; the rappel line drops from there into the east-face basin. Anchors are natural — trees, horns and slings — so carry cord and webbing to back up or replace what you find. Expect a mix of downclimbing and one or two double-rope rappels depending on how much snow is in the gully.

waypoints.name: Alpental / Snow Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Self-serve day-use fee kiosk (Northwest Forest Pass or $5/day); trail departs the north end of the upper Alpental Ski Area parking lot.
waypoints.directions: From I-90 Exit 52, follow Alpental Road to its end and park in the upper Alpental lot (~3,100 ft). The trail leaves from the north end of the lot. Self-serve fee kiosk — Northwest Forest Pass or $5/day.

waypoints.name: Source Lake Trail junction
waypoints.note: Leave the maintained Snow Lake Trail here toward Source Lake and Chair's east basin.
waypoints.directions: The first half mile follows the old ski-area cat track before it becomes standard trail, then climbs gently through forest. Stay on the maintained Snow Lake Trail until the Source Lake fork — that is where you leave it.

waypoints.name: Thumb Tack
waypoints.note: Large rock landmark in Chair's east basin; skis or packs are often cached here before ascending toward the buttress.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail at the fork and continue cross-country on boot path toward the basin under Chair's east face, roughly half a mile to a mile of talus, heather and (early or mid season) snow. The Thumb Tack is the large rock landmark once you are in the basin; parties commonly cache skis or packs here.

waypoints.name: Buttress base / entry gully
waypoints.note: Blocky entry gully gains low-angle blocky rock leading toward the buttress prow; rope up here for the exposed Class 4 to 5.4 climbing above.
waypoints.directions: From the Thumb Tack climb a short snow gully, about 300 ft, to gain the crest of the ridge that forms the Northeast Buttress. This gully sits under avalanche terrain coming off Chair and Snoqualmie Mountain and is a known early-season slide path — most parties carry axe and crampons from the basin onward and rope up at the base of the blocky entry gully.

waypoints.name: Tree cluster near buttress prow
waypoints.note: Notable stand of trees used as a belay stance on the ascent and as the first rappel anchor on the descent.
waypoints.directions: Follow the ridge crest up low-angle blocky rock from the entry gully to the stand of trees on the prow. This is the usual belay stance on the way up, and the first rappel anchor on the way down.

waypoints.name: Chair Peak summit
waypoints.note: True summit is the uncorniced center section with rock underneath; the northeast side is heavily corniced.
waypoints.directions: Continue up the buttress — four to five pitches of class 3-4 with big exposure. The true summit is the uncorniced centre section with rock underneath it; the northeast side is heavily corniced, so stay well back from the lip.

waypoints.name: Notch/saddle in main ridge
waypoints.note: Downclimb the SE-facing gully from the true summit to this notch before the rappels; steep unconsolidated snow up to about 70 degrees.
waypoints.directions: Descending: from the true summit, downclimb the southeast-facing gully to the notch in the main ridge. Steep unconsolidated snow, up to roughly 70 degrees.

waypoints.name: Fixed rappel anchor at rock buttress
waypoints.note: Double-rope rappel from a fixed anchor here down to the tree cluster, then continue rappelling and downclimbing to the base of the buttress.
waypoints.directions: From the notch, continue to the fixed anchor on the rock buttress. A double-rope rappel from here reaches the tree cluster, then keep rappelling and downclimbing to the base of the buttress and reverse the approach.

waypoints.name: Stuart Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Northwest Forest Pass required for parking; day trips self-issue a free permit at the kiosk; camping overnight May 15-Oct 31 needs an Enchantment overnight (quota) permit.
waypoints.directions: From US 2 at the west edge of Leavenworth, turn south onto Icicle Road and drive 8.4 miles, then turn left onto FS Road 7601 and follow this rough dirt road 3.7 miles to its end at the Stuart Lake Trailhead, about 3,400 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park, and day trips need the free self-issued permit at the trailhead.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Lake / Stuart Lake Trail split
waypoints.note: Signed junction where trail flattens briefly; bear left (south) onto Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A, Stuart Lake Trail continues straight.
waypoints.directions: Follow the Stuart Lake Trail about 2.25 miles through forest along Mountaineer Creek, crossing it on a log bridge near the 1.5-mile mark, to the signed junction where the Colchuck Lake Trail splits left.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Lake
waypoints.note: Trail tops out on a broad granite slab over the lake; last reliable, easy-access water before the route.
waypoints.directions: Turn left onto the Colchuck Lake Trail, cross Mountaineer Creek again on a second log bridge, and climb increasingly steep, rocky switchbacks about 1.75 miles to a broad granite slab overlooking the lake.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Lake outlet crossing
waypoints.note: Cross the outlet at the lake's north end, at or just below the small dam; a real crossing, not a step-across, in early season.
waypoints.directions: Where the trail meets the lake, take the left fork and stay high, ignoring the spurs that drop to the water, to the small dam at the lake's north end. Cross the outlet creek on or just below the dam.

waypoints.name: Talus cirque below the West Face
waypoints.note: Boulder-hop the cirque basin below the wall; loose talus and route-finding through the cairned climbers' path to the obvious crack system.
waypoints.directions: On the far side of the outlet, follow the well-cairned climbers' path up and across the timbered hillside; it gains height quickly and puts you on the talus field below the West Face in about an hour. Snow can linger on this ground into early summer.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Balanced Rock summit
waypoints.note: Final moves are an exposed V1 boulder problem to mantel onto the nesting summit block.
waypoints.directions: Boulder-hop the cirque to a left-facing, lightly vegetated corner at the foot of the wall and scramble up to a ledge where the first pitch starts; if you are under black streaks or a large pale rock scar you are too far right. Climb nine pitches of sustained cracks and corners, finishing with an exposed boulder move to mantel onto the summit block.

waypoints.name: Summit rappel station
waypoints.note: Single ~30m rappel off a slung horn near the summit; rope can hang up in the sling if pulled from the wrong angle, then downclimb scree clockwise around the peak.
waypoints.directions: From the summit block, scramble to the webbing-slung horn on its east side for the single 30 m rappel.

waypoints.name: Goodell Creek Trail Trailhead (climbers' access near Upper Group Campground)
waypoints.directions: Park at the Goodell Creek Group Campground on SR-20 near Newhalem, at about 600 feet. The climbers' path begins behind a large boulder at the back of the Upper Group Campground. If you'll be camping in Terror Basin, North Cascades National Park requires a backcountry camping permit — pick it up in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center (walk-up only, no advance reservations for this zone).

waypoints.name: Cairn / Terror Basin Route split
waypoints.note: Cairn marks where the climbers' path leaves the old logging roadbed and angles south of Terror Creek, climbing steeply toward treeline.
waypoints.directions: Walk the old Goodell Creek roadbed upvalley about 3.5-4 miles, brushy with deadfall and a handful of washouts, to the cairn near 1,700 ft. Two creek crossings low on the path can run high and fast on hot afternoons.

waypoints.name: Notch above Terror Basin
waypoints.note: The path tops out at a notch in the ridge, the first view into Terror Basin and across to the Pickets; the gully down the far side to camp is steep and loose.
waypoints.directions: Leave the roadbed at the cairn and climb steeply up the timbered spur south of Terror Creek, past about 3,200 ft, then up heather benches and slabs above treeline to a notch in the ridge at about 6,200 ft.

waypoints.name: Terror Basin Camp
waypoints.note: Gravelly, wildflower-covered basin with established tent sites and running snowmelt streams — the standard high camp shared by parties climbing any of the McMillan Spires.
waypoints.directions: Descend the steep, loose gully on the far side of the notch to the flat gravelly tent sites of Terror Basin at about 5,800 ft, with running snowmelt water.

waypoints.name: Snow gully below East-West McMillan col
waypoints.note: Steep snow/scree gully estimated in the 40-degree range on the approach to the col — crampons and axe essential; this is also the descent line, so watch for rockfall and parties below.
waypoints.directions: From camp, traverse benches, trending slightly downhill, to the outlet of the glacial lake near 5,500 ft. Cross the outlet, climb slabs and snow onto the Terror Glacier, and head for the gully that rises to the col between West and East McMillan Spires.

waypoints.name: East-West McMillan Col
waypoints.note: Crux decision point where the steep snow gully and the 4th-class rock ledge variant both top out before the final scramble to the East summit block.
waypoints.directions: Climb the gully, which steepens to about 40 degrees for its last 200-300 ft, or take the reddish, rightward-trending ledges and short 4th-class rib on its true-left side to the same col.

waypoints.name: East McMillan Spire Summit
waypoints.directions: From the col, scramble the exposed 3rd-class ridge crest east to the summit.

waypoints.name: Thunder Creek Trailhead, Colonial Creek Campground
waypoints.note: Trail starts at the amphitheater in the campground's south loop off SR 20 (MP 130); NPS backcountry permit required for the overnight bivy.
waypoints.directions: The trailhead is at Colonial Creek Campground on SR 20, just past milepost 130 — turn into the campground and find the trail starting at the amphitheater in the south loop, at about 1,200 feet. A North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, available from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, is required for the overnight bivy at the Borealis Glacier.

waypoints.name: Colonial Creek South Campground, Thunder Creek trailhead
McAllister Camp
waypoints.note: Established NPS camp where McAllister Creek meets Thunder Creek; last easy, reliable water before leaving the valley floor.
waypoints.directions: Follow the Thunder Creek Trail south up the valley, roughly 6 to 6.7 easy miles for only about 700 ft of gain. The footbridge that once crossed Thunder Creek near the camp is gone, so expect a log crossing or a wade, and check current park trail conditions before you go.

waypoints.name: Leave the trail for Lucky Ridge
waypoints.note: A social trail drops about 50 ft from the Thunder Creek Trail toward the creek here; this is where climbers leave the maintained trail, cross Thunder Creek, and start up Lucky Ridge toward Primus.
waypoints.directions: Continue south on the Thunder Creek Trail about a third to half a mile past McAllister Camp, to where a social trail drops steeply about 50 ft toward Thunder Creek. Leave the maintained trail here; Tricouni Camp, about a mile farther up the valley, is not on this route.

waypoints.name: Bivy at toe of Borealis Glacier
waypoints.note: Gravel bivy spots on the old streambed near the proglacial lake at the glacier's terminus, with a direct view of the icefall above; reached by climbing SSE up Lucky Ridge from the Thunder Creek crossing.
waypoints.directions: Leave the valley trail on a short steep drop toward Thunder Creek and cross the creek before picking up the climbers' path on the far side; the first quarter to half mile is a bushwhack through devil's club and blowdown before the boot track becomes usable. It then climbs the ridge dividing McAllister and Thunder creeks, gaining roughly 4,000 ft in about two miles of steep forest, slide alder and finally larch and heather, to treeline and the gravel flats beside the lake at the glacier's toe.

waypoints.name: Borealis Glacier icefall
waypoints.note: Rope up at the bivy and stay on the glacier's eastern margin here — the lower and upper tiers are split by an icefall and cliff bands that have caught parties climbing too far climber's-left.
waypoints.directions: Rope up before stepping onto the ice. The glacier has retreated into a lower and an upper tier separated by an icefall and cliff bands, and picking the line that links them is the crux of the day; parties that commit to the wrong side get cliffed out above the lower tier. Scout it from the bivy in good light rather than working it out on the move.

waypoints.name: Lucky Pass (Primus-Tricouni col)
waypoints.note: Gain the col via the glacier's east margin; the East Ridge to Primus's summit starts here, with the Tricouni Peak route splitting off to the east.
waypoints.directions: Continue up the upper tier to the broad snow col between Primus and Tricouni at about 7,200 ft, weaving around crevasses. Moats open where the snow pulls back from rock later in the season, so test the edges before stepping across.

waypoints.name: Primus Peak
waypoints.note: True summit reached via 3rd-class scrambling along the East Ridge from Lucky Pass; descent reverses the same ridge and glacier line.
waypoints.directions: From the col turn up the ridge toward Primus, about 1,300 ft of Class 2-3 talus, scree and snow with no defined path. Where it steepens below a false summit around 8,270 ft, traverse climber's left around it rather than taking the steep snow head-on, then finish on easy blocks and a short run of kicked steps. The rock is loose enough that helmets matter more here than the grade implies.

removed.wp: Leave the trail for Lucky Ridge

waypoints.name: Stuart Lake Trailhead
waypoints.directions: From US-2 at the west edge of Leavenworth, turn onto Icicle Creek Road and drive about 8.4 miles, then turn left onto FS Road 7601 (Eightmile Road) and follow the potholed gravel road about 3.7 miles to its end at the Stuart Lake Trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass is required; day visitors self-issue a free Enchantment permit at the trailhead, and overnight stays need a lottery permit. FS Road 7601 is closed in winter, typically November to May.

waypoints.name: Stuart Lake Trailhead (end of FR 7601)
waypoints.directions: From US-2 at the western edge of Leavenworth, take Icicle Creek Road 8.4 miles and turn left onto FR 7601. Follow the bumpy dirt road 3.7 miles to the Stuart Lake Trailhead at its end (about 3,400 ft). A Northwest Forest Pass is required, plus a self-issued day-use permit; overnight camping at Colchuck Lake needs an Enchantments permit.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Lake (north end)
waypoints.directions: Take Trail #1599, crossing Mountaineer Creek on a log bridge at about 1.5 miles. At the junction where the Stuart Lake trail continues, take the Colchuck Lake Trail, recross the creek on a second log bridge, and climb steep, rocky trail to the north end of the lake at about 5,560 ft, 4 miles from the car.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Balanced Rock summit block
waypoints.directions: Follow the trail along the west shore to the boulder field at the south end, then take the cairned Aasgard Pass climbers' path up talus and heather to about 400 ft above the lake. Cut climber's left through 15-20 minutes of slide alder and heather to the gully below Colchuck Balanced Rock; Full Tilt starts a few hundred feet down the gully, right of the West Face start, after a loose 3rd/4th-class scramble. Five pitches lead to the summit ridge.

waypoints.name: Wolf Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Parking area off Left Fork Wolf Creek Road (FS 5505); Northwest Forest Pass required, no wilderness permit needed.
waypoints.directions: The Wolf Creek Trailhead is a large parking area at the end of FS Road 5505 (Left Fork Wolf Creek Road) above Winthrop, at about 2,900 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required; no wilderness permit is needed. Check current Wolf Creek Road conditions before you drive in. Most parties come mid-July through September, once the trail and the upper basins are snow-free.

waypoints.name: North Fork Wolf Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Crossing of the North Fork — a fire-damaged log bridge, and in early season a difficult, hazardous ford; reliable water here.
waypoints.directions: Wolf Creek Trail #527 drops about 250 ft out of the trailhead, then settles into a long, gently graded valley-bottom walk into the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness. Nearly all of this stretch burned in the 2021 Cedar Creek Fire, so expect blackened deadfall, standing dead snags and almost no shade — a real overhead hazard in wind. The North Fork crossing is a couple of miles in and can run high in early season.

waypoints.name: Gardner Meadows
waypoints.note: Three established campsites in fire-cleared, avalanche-scoured meadow terrain along Wolf Creek; the standard basecamp for the summit push.
waypoints.directions: Continue straight up the Wolf Creek valley for roughly another eight miles of easy, gradually rising trail, still through burn the whole way. The Abernathy Lake trail splits off around seven and a half miles in — stay on the valley trail. The meadows open out over about a mile; water runs through them and the established camps are here.

waypoints.name: Off-trail turnoff toward the Gardner/North Gardner basin
waypoints.note: Leave the maintained Wolf Creek Trail here, staying west of the small stream draining south off Gardner Mountain, and climb toward the basin below the two peaks.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail at the meadows and start cross-country toward the peak, staying on the west bank of the small stream that drains south off Gardner. Grassy benches lead up to a small meadow basin below the two peaks.

waypoints.name: Scree/talus crux slope
waypoints.note: About 1,400 ft of gain in a half mile of loose, marble-sized scree and sand below the ridge crest — a slow 'one step forward, two steps back' grind.
waypoints.directions: Above the basin the ground turns to loose, marble-sized scree over sand — roughly 1,400 ft of gain in about half a mile, slow going with a faint climber's path that is easy to lose. Into early summer, snow patches linger on this slope and are worth an ice axe.

waypoints.name: Connecting saddle below Point 8,487
waypoints.note: Saddle between Gardner and North Gardner where the ridge route to Gardner's summit begins; also the reversal point on descent back down the northwest ridge.
waypoints.directions: Keep grinding up the scree, threading a few short cliff bands and gullies, to top out on the ridge crest. This stretch is the route-finding crux of the approach and the rock underfoot stays loose the whole way.

waypoints.name: Gardner Mountain summit
waypoints.note: Broad, gentle summit on the ridge crest, second-highest peak of the Methow Mountains; open ridge is exposed to lightning in afternoon storms.
waypoints.directions: From the saddle, follow the ridge to the true summit: easier walking on broken rock with occasional hand-holds and brief exposure near the top, class 2-3. The summit is broad and fully open, with no shelter if afternoon storms build.

waypoints.name: North Fork Sauk River Trailhead
waypoints.note: Northwest Forest Pass required at the kiosk; this has been the primary approach since the White Chuck River Trail washed out in 2003.
waypoints.directions: The North Fork Sauk River Trailhead sits at about 2,050 ft off FR 49, the Sloan Creek Road, and it is where Trail #649 starts up the valley. A Northwest Forest Pass is required, and there is a kiosk at the trailhead. Do not plan on coming in from the west: the White Chuck River Road (FR 23) remains washed out, and this has been the primary approach to Glacier Peak since the White Chuck River Trail washed out in 2003.

waypoints.name: Mackinaw Shelter (former shelter site)
waypoints.note: Old-growth riverside camp; the actual shelter is gone/unsafe, use the established sites nearby, last reliable flat camping before the climb steepens.
waypoints.directions: Follow the North Fork Sauk trail up-valley on a mellow, rolling, well-maintained grade through old-growth forest, with a few scattered campsites along the way. The old shelter site is the last of the low-elevation river camps; past it the trail leaves the valley floor and steepens sharply.

waypoints.name: North Fork Sauk Trail / PCT junction near White Pass
waypoints.note: Trail gains ~3,000 ft in the final stretch to this meadow junction with sweeping views of Glacier Peak; join the PCT here.
waypoints.directions: Beyond the old shelter site the trail turns into roughly three miles of switchbacks, gaining about 3,000 ft to the meadows at White Pass. Water is unreliable once you leave the river, so fill up before starting the climb. The PCT junction is at the top.

waypoints.name: Foam Creek Trail / ridge saddle crossing
waypoints.note: Leave the PCT on the Foam Creek climbers' path and cross the ridge saddle into the White Chuck Glacier basin.
waypoints.directions: From the PCT at White Pass, take the Foam Creek climbers' trail east for about two miles, then cross the ridge at a saddle on its north side near 6,600 ft. This saddle is the end of trail travel — beyond it the route is open basin and snow.

waypoints.name: White Chuck Glacier basin crossing
waypoints.note: Open glacial basin traverse trending NE toward Glacier Gap; rope up here as crevasses can be present even though the grade is gentle.
waypoints.directions: Drop north off the saddle into the open White Chuck Glacier basin and trend northeast across it. The grade is gentle, but it is glacier under the snow, so rope up before you start across rather than partway.

waypoints.name: Glacier Gap
waypoints.note: Large, popular camp area with many established sites on a broad gap; standard base camp for the Gerdine Ridge/Cool Glacier route.
waypoints.directions: Continue northeast across the basin, gaining a few hundred feet to the broad gap where the White Chuck and Suiattle glaciers meet. Established sites are spread across the gap, and it is the last flat ground before the summit push.

waypoints.name: Cool Glacier saddle (Gerdine-Cool col)
waypoints.note: Saddle between Disappointment Peak and Glacier Peak where the Gerdine Ridge route tops out onto the Cool Glacier for the final push.
waypoints.directions: Leave camp on crampons, losing a little height onto rocky Gerdine Ridge, then climb north, contouring the slope below Glacier Gap Peak before regaining the crest and following it to roughly 8,400 ft. The climber's track ends near a gendarme around 8,500 ft — rope up there, traverse northeast onto the Gerdine and upper Suiattle ice, and end-run one or two crevasses where it bends into the Cool Glacier. Keep moving on that traverse; the cliffs of Disappointment Peak above it shed rock. Finish by climbing west up the Cool Glacier to regain the ridge at the saddle.

waypoints.name: Glacier Peak summit
waypoints.note: True summit of Glacier Peak (Dakobed); broad volcanic summit with views across the North Cascades.
waypoints.directions: From the saddle the glacier travel is over. Rejoin the climber's trail and finish up one short, steep pitch of pumice and broken volcanic rock to the top — unroped class 2-3, with no rock gear needed.

removed.wp: Foam Creek Trail / ridge saddle crossing

waypoints.name: NF-6514-410 road's end
waypoints.note: Park at the end of spur 410 off Eagle Creek Road (FS-6514), which leaves Beckler River Road (FS-65): about five miles in, keep on 410 at the fork and continue past the Eagle Lake trailhead to the road's end; no maintained trail beyond this point.
waypoints.directions: From US-2 at Skykomish, turn north on Beckler River Road (FS-65). After about 0.8 mile turn left onto FS-6510, and in about a mile turn onto Eagle Creek Road (FS-6514). About five miles in, keep on spur 410 at the fork and continue past the Eagle Lake trailhead to the road's end, a small pullout at about 3,480 ft; the road gets rockier just before it ends. Roughly 6.5 miles of gravel and dirt from pavement; check road status with the Skykomish Ranger District before committing to it.

waypoints.name: Brushy drainage / streambed
waypoints.note: Route starts by climbing a mossy, brush-choked streambed that is slick when wet; poor footing before the terrain opens.
waypoints.directions: There is no trail from the car; the line goes straight into thick huckleberry toward the talus above. Rather than fighting the brush, drop into the streambed running alongside it, which is much easier going even though the rock underfoot is slick.

waypoints.name: Saddle east of Grotto Lake basin
waypoints.note: Huckleberry-covered saddle where the route angles right off the drainage onto the ridge proper before contouring toward Klinger Ridge.
waypoints.directions: Follow the drainage and the talus beside it up into the rock basin around 4,300 ft. Route-finding is entirely on you here, with no trail and no markers, and morning fog frequently sits in this basin well past sunrise, so carry a track you can navigate to.

waypoints.name: Klinger Ridge meadow gain
waypoints.note: Meadowy ridge crest reached via a rising talus traverse; fog commonly lingers here into mid-morning, obscuring the correct line.
waypoints.directions: From the rock basin around 4,300 ft, make a rising traverse across talus into a gully, then climb a heathered slope beneath a cliff band, which dodges a slide-alder tangle, to reach the open meadow crest above 4,600 ft. A cairn near here has pulled parties off the direct line; staying in the gully to about 4,800 ft is the more direct way.

waypoints.name: Notch below summit tower
waypoints.note: Steep talus leads to a notch west of a prominent rock tower; a short vertical downclimb on the south side is exposed and helmet-recommended.
waypoints.directions: Follow the meadow and boulder crest upward, but do not try to hold the literal east ridge crest, which cliffs out and does not go as a through-route. From about 4,800 ft, weave up through steep granite blocks and cross a final talus field to reach the notch.

waypoints.name: Grotto Mountain summit
waypoints.note: Class 4 scramble up a final gully off the notch gains the summit block; views south into the Bolt Creek Fire-burned drainage and across to Mount Baring.
waypoints.directions: Downclimb the short, steep, near-vertical step on the south side of the notch. This is the most exposed move on the route and the rock is loose in places. Then move a short way west into the gully below the summit block and scramble Class 3-4 to the top.

waypoints.name: Rachel Lake Trailhead
waypoints.directions: Take I-90 to Exit 62 (Kachess Lake), turn left off the ramp and follow FR 49 (Kachess Lake Road) toward Kachess Lake. Follow the signs toward Lake Kachess Campground and turn left on FR 4930 (Box Canyon Road), which ends at a large lot and the Rachel Lake trailhead about 4 miles from the turn, around 2,800 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required, plus a free self-issue wilderness permit.

waypoints.name: Hibox Mountain Summit
waypoints.directions: Follow Rachel Lake Trail #1313 about 2 miles to a brushy avalanche clearing near 3,300 ft; just past it take the unmarked climbers' path uphill on the right. Pass the first cliff band on the right, go left around an outcrop, and take a gully on the right through the second band. Climb the meadow and talus to the south side of the summit block, traverse east to the east-side gully, and climb its short class 3 notch to the top.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of the 23-mile Cascade River Road out of Marblemount; NPS wilderness permit (with bear canister for overnight) required, no day-use fee inside the park.
waypoints.directions: The final miles of Cascade River Road out of Marblemount are unpaved and washboarded, and high clearance or AWD makes the drive to the road end considerably easier.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass
waypoints.note: Trail crests the pass and turns east toward Pelton/Horseshoe Basin; a signed spur drops 1 mi and 800 ft to Doubtful Lake below the Sahale Arm.
waypoints.directions: Take the Cascade Pass Trail's well-graded switchbacks up the valley headwall, about 1,800 ft of gain on the only fully maintained tread of the route. Everything above the pass is unmaintained, loose and cairn-marked by comparison, so cover this section efficiently.

waypoints.name: Sahale Glacier Camp
waypoints.note: Highest established backcountry camp in the park, at the base of Sahale Glacier; wind-wall rock sites, reservable NPS permit required, snowmelt water only early season.
waypoints.directions: Continue past the pass junction onto the Sahale Arm Trail and climb the open heather ridge, passing the Doubtful Lake overlook, to the camp at the toe of the glacier. It is a steady 2,200 ft of exposed, shadeless climbing with no water until you reach camp.

waypoints.name: Secret Gully descent off Sahale Arm
waypoints.note: Climbers' descent gully dropping east off the Sahale Arm into Horseshoe Basin; loose rock on slabs and unstable underfoot once snow-free.
waypoints.directions: From camp, traverse east across the boulder-and-heather plateau below the glacier, passing the dozen or so established camp pads, then downclimb a steep snowfield that can stay firm or icy into midsummer — an axe or whippet earns its place here. Traverse east again to gain Sahale Peak's sharp southeast ridge, then follow the cairned climbers' trail down the ridge over one short 4th-class step to where the gully drops away east.

waypoints.name: Horseshoe Basin staging area
waypoints.note: Waterfall-lined cirque beneath Ripsaw Ridge between Boston Peak and Buckner; stage here before the scramble up to Horseshoe Peak's south-facing gully.
waypoints.directions: Descend the scree-and-talus gully to the snowfield at about 6,600 ft and cross it into the basin. Melted out, the gully is loose mostly-3rd-class ground that needs real care; with snow still in it the concern shifts to steep firm snow instead. In the basin, traverse the wide ledge at roughly 6,600 ft as it rises toward the ruins of the old Black Warrior mine near 6,800 ft. Do not drink the basin's water — it drains historic mine tailings, so carry what you need from Doubtful Creek or camp.

waypoints.name: Summit gully and ledge
waypoints.note: 30-45° loose gully climbs to a ledge about 100 ft below the true summit, directly below the final 5.2 notch.
waypoints.directions: Contour northeast and then east on loose scree, talus and slabs below the Davenport Glacier to reach the base of Ripsaw Ridge under the peak, then start up the Class 3 dike-and-gully system. A short Class 4 step breaks it partway up. The whole line is loose enough that another party above you is the main hazard, so wear a helmet and keep the group either tight or well out of the fall line.

waypoints.name: Horseshoe Peak
waypoints.note: True summit gained by ~5 ft of 5th-class climbing to a one-meter-square notch (feels overhung but isn't); downclimb or single-rope rappel to reverse.
waypoints.directions: From the ledge, scramble about 10 ft of Class 3/4 onto a ledge that angles diagonally up the south face to an obvious cleft just below the top, exiting on loose Class 3/4 rock at the notch. The final moves are 5.2 over fall-would-be-fatal exposure, so most parties rope the ramp as one pitch of roughly 30 m and belay off the horn on the east side of the notch. That horn is also the rappel anchor on the way down; it is natural rock with no fixed hardware, so carry a few cams in case the sling is missing or worn.

removed.wp: Secret Gully descent off Sahale Arm

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of Cascade River Road (FR-15), 23.1 mi from Marblemount; day use is free but overnight parties need a North Cascades NP backcountry permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.
waypoints.directions: Cascade River Road runs roughly 23 miles from Marblemount, pavement giving way to gravel for the upper half. The last gravel section is gated through the winter and typically does not open until the snow clears, often not until late June or July, so confirm the road is open all the way to the end before committing to the drive.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass
waypoints.note: High point of the maintained trail; camping is prohibited at the pass itself, so continue toward Pelton Basin or contour east/south toward Cache Glacier.
waypoints.directions: Follow the well-graded, heavily used Cascade Pass Trail about 3.7 miles and 1,800 ft, switchbacking up through forest and avalanche-path meadows to the pass. The last reliable trailside water is at the creek crossings low on the trail, so fill bottles before starting the switchbacks.

waypoints.name: Pelton Basin Camp
waypoints.note: Wooded basin camp on Pelton Creek just below and east of the pass; reliable water and the last easy legal camp before the cross-country push to Cache Col.
waypoints.directions: From the pass the maintained trail keeps going east, traversing a scree slope and descending into Pelton Basin, with a short signed spur dropping to the camp about a mile from the pass. Water is reliable here, and this is the last easy legal camp before the route leaves the trail.

waypoints.name: Cache Col / Cache Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Rocky gap between Magic Mountain and Mixup Peak at the head of Cache Glacier; cross the glacier here and watch for open crevasses in low-snow late-season conditions.
waypoints.directions: Climb back west to the Cascade Pass area and leave the maintained tread on the climbers' boot track heading south-southeast. It makes a rising traverse over loose ground, heather and firm morning snow patches across Mixup Peak's flanks to the toe of the Cache Glacier near 6,000 ft, then up moderate snow slopes to the notch. Crevasses open here by late summer, so carry a rope and crevasse-rescue kit and be ready to use them.

waypoints.name: Kool-Aid Lake
waypoints.note: Small alpine tarn ~1 mile SSE of Cache Col that serves as the standard day-1 camp for parties climbing Hurry-up Peak or starting the Ptarmigan Traverse; often still snow/ice-covered into August.
waypoints.directions: From the col drop and traverse south-southeast about a mile over loose rock, heather benches and occasional snowfields to the tarn. It is the only dependable water in the basin and can still be partly frozen early in the season.

waypoints.name: Exposed summit ridge scramble
waypoints.note: Class 2-3 scrambling with moderate exposure along the final summit ridge; early-season parties report steep snow here that warrants pickets for protection.
waypoints.directions: From the lake climb south, over scree, heather and broken granite benches, then take a gully up to the summit ridge. A band of steep snow around 7,100 ft commonly persists into midsummer, so carry an axe and crampons even in August. Route-finding on the benches is the real crux here: several similar-looking gully lines lead up and not all of them are the right one.

waypoints.name: Hurry-up Peak Summit
waypoints.note: True summit (historically also called Ess/S Mountain); open view north to Trapper Lake and the rest of the Ptarmigan Traverse peaks.
waypoints.directions: Once on the summit ridge, follow it past a false summit to the true top, which lies a short way beyond. The scrambling is class 2-3 with moderate exposure, and the rock is loose enough that holds want testing before they are weighted.

waypoints.name: Goodell Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Unmarked pullout off SR-20 behind a large boulder at Goodell Creek Campground; NPS wilderness permit required for overnight camping in the Terror/Crescent Creek basins.
waypoints.directions: Park at the Goodell Creek trailhead and group campground on SR-20, just west of Newhalem — an unmarked pullout behind a large boulder. If you plan to camp overnight in the Terror Creek or Crescent Creek basins, you'll need an NPS wilderness permit.

waypoints.name: Terror Basin climbers' path cairn
waypoints.note: Old roadbed ends and a rock cairn marks a hard right turnoff onto the steep, more-defined climbers' path, which runs atop a forested ridge here.
waypoints.directions: Walk the old streamside roadbed up the Goodell Creek valley at easy grades for about four miles, crossing the creek along the way. The last flowing water is near 1,600 ft and everything above is dry, so fill up there rather than counting on the basin. Watch the uphill side closely as you go: the turnoff is small, sometimes unmarked, and parties routinely stride past it and waste an hour on the valley trail.

waypoints.name: Terror Basin camp
waypoints.note: Glacial-outwash camping among streams below the Southern Pickets; treeline is passed around 5000-5200 ft on the way up.
waypoints.directions: The path goes straight up the forested hillside with no switchbacks and no let-up, a long haul on roots and dirt that most parties consider the hardest part of the whole approach. There is no water anywhere on it. Timber ends near 5,000-5,200 ft and the ground turns to meadow, slab and usually old snow, from where a rising traverse leads toward a broad saddle and the camping benches just below it.

waypoints.name: The Barrier crossing
waypoints.note: Loose, 'serious Class 3' rock rib separating Terror Basin from Crescent Creek Basin, just below Degenhardt; crossing higher avoids a longer traverse but involves a moat and low-5th-class moves — parties have turned back here. Only needed if continuing to Crescent Creek Basin; this route does not cross it.
waypoints.directions: Work up and across the basin toward Degenhardt to reach the rib. Where you cross it matters more than anything else on this leg — going in low is longer and brushier and has pulled parties onto fifth-class ground, while taking it high near the notch shortens the traverse but usually means dealing with a moat where the snow pulls back from the rock. The rock is loose enough throughout that a slip, not the technical grade, is the real hazard.

waypoints.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp
waypoints.note: Camp in the next basin west, under Mount Terror, reached over the Barrier; it serves parties continuing through the Southern Pickets and is not on the way to this route, which is reached from Terror Basin across the Terror Glacier.
waypoints.directions: From the notch at the top of the rib, drop onto the snow ramp running down the far side, which is an easy descent while it still holds snow and turns into loose talus and open moats as the season goes on. It puts you straight into the basin under Terror at around 6,200 ft.

waypoints.name: West Ridge gain point
waypoints.note: Leave the basin talus/snow and scramble onto the crest of Inspiration's west ridge above camp.
waypoints.directions: Climb the talus and snow out of the basin and cross the glacier below the peak; it is crevassed, and the moat or bergschrund at its head is the usual obstacle in getting onto rock at all. Start up the obvious gully above it and follow that until stepping out onto the crest makes sense, roughly 300 ft above the ice.

waypoints.name: Exposed gneiss ridge steps
waypoints.note: Sequence of exposed 5.7 steps along the ridge crest below the summit block, on much better rock than the lower pitches.
waypoints.directions: The first pitches are the poorest rock on the route: slabby compact ground where anchors are awkward to arrange, a large corner and chimney stacked with loose blocks, and lichen-covered ledge systems leading back toward the crest. Quality improves steadily with every pitch gained. Belay somewhere out of the fall line of what the leader is going to pull off.

waypoints.name: Inspiration Peak
waypoints.note: True summit of Inspiration Peak in the Southern Pickets; descend by rappelling the west ridge crest with a single 60m rope back to the glacier above the moat.
waypoints.directions: Once the crest proper is underfoot the rock turns solid and well featured, and easy fifth class runs a couple of hundred feet to the base of the summit headwall. The last pitches take the headwall itself on good holds, passing a pale rock scar on the way to the top.

waypoints.name: Easy Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: Signed pullout on SR-20 between mileposts 151-152; self-issue Northwest Forest Pass required at the kiosk, ~10-car lot.
waypoints.directions: From Marblemount, drive SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) east about 45 miles and turn right between mileposts 151 and 152 onto the short spur signed for Easy Pass, ending at a lot for about 10 cars. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass is required (self-issue at the kiosk). The highway closes in winter, so the trailhead is reachable only once it opens for the season.

waypoints.name: Easy Pass — leave trail
waypoints.note: Trail crests Easy Pass through open meadows; leave the maintained tread near the first switchback just below the pass to begin the cross-country traverse toward Ragged Ridge.
waypoints.directions: The Easy Pass Trail climbs steadily for about 3.5 miles and 2,800 ft, switchbacking through old-growth forest along Easy Creek before breaking into open meadow at the crest. The upper, north-facing switchbacks hold steep snow well into early summer, so an axe is worth carrying outside of high summer. At the pass, ignore the tread continuing down the far side toward Fisher Creek.

waypoints.name: Waterfall creek crossing
waypoints.note: Traverse descends ~200 ft of steep scree to cross a waterfall-fed creek — last reliable water before camp.
waypoints.directions: From the pass, sidehill west along the south side of Ragged Ridge, roughly holding the 6,600-6,700 ft contour over talus and heather benches and across a series of small gullies and minor rock buttresses. Traversing too high is the standard mistake on this stretch and it will cliff you out above the drainage, so give up height early rather than late. Route-finding here, not the climbing, is the crux of the approach.

waypoints.name: Ragged Ridge Camp
waypoints.note: Established bivy sites in the basin just south of Mesahchie Peak; usually has water in the basin; roughly 5 hours in from the trailhead.
waypoints.directions: Past the creek, regain the contour and keep west below Mesahchie Peak for another half mile into the basin holding the camps. Water comes from snowmelt streams and the waterfall drainage nearby, both of which can dry up late in the season.

waypoints.name: 7,400 ft bench
waypoints.note: Climb ~800 ft above camp to a broad bench and start the long ascending traverse west, staying above the lower gully bands toward Kimtah.
waypoints.directions: Gain the bench directly above camp on heather and broken granite and slate. Fill up in the basin first — there is no reliable water past this point once the snowmelt streams fade, and everything above is trail-less cross-country travel.

waypoints.name: Grotesque Gendarmes cliff band
waypoints.note: Crux of the approach: downclimb 250-300 ft of exposed 4th-class rock around a buttress/cliff below a cluster of gendarmes on airy ledges — worse if wet or snow-covered.
waypoints.directions: Traverse west along the bench at roughly 7,400-7,600 ft, crossing more than a dozen loose ribs and gullies on mostly class 3 ground. A distinct reddish ledge cuts across the ribs at about this level and, once found, removes most of the route-finding; losing it turns this section into hours of climbing in and out of gullies. It runs to the base of the gendarmes, where a cliff band blocks further traversing.

waypoints.name: Water-filled summit gully
waypoints.note: Past the gendarmes, find the third major gully (often holds meltwater/snow) and climb its solid-granite class 3 rock to gain the ridge just west of the summit.
waypoints.directions: Past the gendarme bypass the ledge system threads a cliffy, cave-like section before opening onto the gullies below the summit. Count them carefully and scope the line from a distance if you can — several parallel gullies look alike from below and taking the wrong one is the most commonly reported error here. If you want a rope through this ground, bring slings for natural anchors: the fractured granite and slate offer nothing fixed and no obvious solid blocks.

waypoints.name: Kimtah Peak
waypoints.note: True summit on Ragged Ridge; final push is class 3 scrambling east along the ridge crest from the gully topout, with Kimtah and Katsuk Glaciers visible below.
waypoints.directions: Climb the gully on solid class 3 granite, often holding snow or meltwater, to the ridge crest, then cross the scree saddle and scramble class 3 rock along the crest to the true (east) summit.

waypoints.name: Monument Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk; no water/restrooms on-site; trail 484 starts off FR 5400 near the end of Lost River Road.
waypoints.directions: From SR 20 about 14 miles west of Winthrop, turn onto Lost River Road (County Road 9140) and follow it through Mazama to the end of the pavement at about 7.5 miles, where it becomes Harts Pass Road (FS 5400). In about a quarter mile turn right into the Monument Creek Trailhead at about 2,400 ft. No parking pass is needed; self-issue a free wilderness permit at the kiosk.

waypoints.name: Eureka Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Footlog/ford where the old bridge has repeatedly washed out; last reliable water for the next ~8 miles and 5,000 ft of climbing up Pistol Ridge.
waypoints.directions: Trail 484 runs north up the Lost River valley for about four miles of easy walking — the only maintained stretch of trail on the whole trip. The unbridged crossing is the one real hazard on this leg: during June and early-July runoff it can run thigh- to waist-deep, so cross in the cool of the morning when flows are lowest and be prepared to turn around rather than force it.

waypoints.name: Abandoned Pistol Ridge trail split
waypoints.note: Here the route leaves the valley and follows the old, unmaintained Pistol Pass trail steeply onto the crest of Pistol Ridge.
waypoints.directions: Fill every bottle at the creek — there is no reliable water from here until the lake basin, roughly eight miles and 5,000 ft of climbing away. Beyond the crossing the tread degrades into an abandoned trail climbing steeply out of the valley, with heavy deadfall, brush, and stretches where the path disappears entirely and cairns are all you have to follow.

waypoints.name: Pistol Ridge crest side-hill
waypoints.note: Exposed, poorly-defined tread along the ridge crest with steep drop-offs; easy to lose the path in fog or early-season snow.
waypoints.directions: Climb steeply onto the ridge crest, about 1,800 ft over two and a half miles on faint, unmaintained tread. Expect to lose the path repeatedly in blowdown and brush and to navigate by cairn and map rather than by tread.

waypoints.name: Pistol Pass
waypoints.note: High saddle on Pistol Ridge marking the top of the approach; from here the route drops off-trail toward Lake of the Woods and Monument-Lake basin.
waypoints.directions: Continue along the crest to the saddle, another 900 ft of gain spread over roughly three miles, picking up cairns where the tread fades out. This tops out the approach climb — from the creek ford it is about 5,000 ft of gain, all of it dry.

waypoints.name: Lake of the Woods
waypoints.note: Small alpine lake between Lake and Pistol Peaks with several established campsites; primary water source and base camp for the summit day.
waypoints.directions: Drop off the far side of the pass and follow the basin about a mile north past the lake to the established camps. This is the first water since the creek ford. Parties commonly arrive here after dark at the end of a nine-hour-plus day, so know where the camps sit before you get close.

waypoints.name: Lake Mountain east ridge gain point
waypoints.note: Leave camp and gain Lake Mountain's east ridge directly above the lake basin; loose but solid granite, Class 2-3 with some exposure.
waypoints.directions: From camp, climb northwest straight out of the lake basin through the larches toward the lower east ridge. Do not try to go straight up the peak's south side — a subsidiary rock knob (Point 8165) and a cliff band near 8,000 ft bar a direct line, which is why the route swings around to the east ridge. All of this is off-trail talus, scree, and boulder-field travel.

waypoints.name: Lake Mountain
waypoints.note: True summit; broad, rocky top with views across the Pasayten toward Monument Peak and the Lost River drainage.
waypoints.directions: Follow the east ridge over blocky granite through larches and boulder fields, mostly Class 2 with occasional exposed Class 2-3 moves. Where the summit ridge meets the southeast slopes there is a short, roughly half-pitch stretch of genuinely exposed Class 3 that reads harder downclimbing than climbing, so note your line as you pass it. Stay on the crest or its south side and well clear of the north wall and northeast face, which are much steeper and not part of this route.

waypoints.name: Stuart Lake Trailhead (FR 7601)
waypoints.directions: From US 2 at the western edge of Leavenworth, turn onto Icicle Creek Road and drive 8.4 miles, then turn left onto Forest Road 7601 and follow the bumpy dirt road 3.7 miles to the Stuart Lake Trailhead at its end. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass is required to park, and a free self-issued permit covers a day trip; overnight stays need an Enchantments permit.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Lake — last reliable water
waypoints.directions: Hike the Colchuck Lake Trail through forest along Mountaineer Creek, crossing it on a log bridge near 1.5 miles. At the signed junction take the Colchuck Lake fork, then climb steepening rocky switchbacks and a boulder moraine to the lake, about 4 miles and 2,280 ft of gain. Fill water here.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Balanced Rock summit
waypoints.directions: Continue along the lake toward its south end onto the cairned Aasgard Pass climbers' trail and climb talus and heather to about 400 ft above the lake. Cut climber's left through a dense band of slide alder and heather to the base gully below the rock, then scramble loose 3rd and 4th class terrain to the start on the left side of the wall, near Scarface. Five pitches lead to the summit block, the last a long traverse up and left.

waypoints.name: Stuart Lake Trailhead (end of FR 7601)
waypoints.directions: From US 2 at the western edge of Leavenworth, turn onto Icicle Creek Road and drive 8.4 miles, then turn left onto Forest Road 7601 and follow the bumpy dirt road 3.7 miles to the Stuart Lake Trailhead at its end, at about 3,400 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass is required to park, and a free self-issued permit covers a day trip; overnight stays need an Enchantments permit.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Lake (outlet / north dam crossing)
waypoints.directions: Hike the Colchuck Lake Trail through forest along Mountaineer Creek, crossing it on a log bridge near 1.5 miles. At the signed junction take the Colchuck Lake fork, cross the creek again on a log bridge, then climb steepening rocky switchbacks and a boulder moraine to the lake outlet, about 4 miles and 2,280 ft of gain. Fill water here.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Balanced Rock summit block
waypoints.directions: Cross the outlet and follow the lakeshore path toward Aasgard Pass, climbing talus and heather to about 400 ft above the lake. Cut left through dense brush to the obvious base gully below the rock, then scramble a 3rd-class ramp out of the gully to the start, which shares the West Face's first pitch. Nine pitches lead to the summit ridge.

waypoints.name: Goodell Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Standard, single approach for all Southern Pickets/Terror Basin objectives including Little Mac Spire.
waypoints.directions: From SR-20 at Newhalem, turn north onto the gravel road across the highway from the Newhalem Campground and follow signs toward the Goodell Creek group camp; park at the small turnout at the trailhead just before the camp.

waypoints.name: Goodell Creek Crossings
waypoints.note: Trail fords two branches of Goodell Creek that run high on hot afternoons; a small streamside campsite sits near the second crossing.
waypoints.directions: Follow the unmaintained but well-trodden climbers' trail north along the old, overgrown logging road bed paralleling Goodell Creek. The walking is forested and comparatively gentle to the creek crossings.

waypoints.name: Terror Creek Cairn / Climbers' Path
waypoints.note: Large cairn and stone arrow mark the turn off the Goodell Creek trail onto the steep, faint climbers' path south of Terror Creek — the start of the '~4,000 ft over 2 mi' push.
waypoints.directions: Continue along the old road bed to its end, where a large cairn and stone arrow mark a hard right turn uphill onto the Terror Basin climbers' path.

waypoints.name: Rocky Streambed Source
waypoints.note: Last dependable water on the climbers' path, running in a rocky streambed; the faint tread resumes just upstream.
waypoints.directions: Turn right and climb the path, which goes brutally steeply more or less straight up the timbered ridge nose between Terror and Crescent Creeks, through brush and a class 3 root-pull cliff band, to the rocky streambed where the last dependable water runs.

waypoints.name: Terror Basin Notch
waypoints.note: Gap on the east rim of Terror Basin reached via a rising traverse over moderate snow into midsummer; first view down onto the basin and the McMillan/Little Mac group.
waypoints.directions: Pick up the faint tread just upstream and make a rising traverse, over moderate snow into midsummer, to the 6,200 ft gap on the east rim of Terror Basin.

waypoints.name: Terror Basin Camp
waypoints.note: Shared high camp for the whole McMillan/Terror cluster — flat gravel benches, running water, and rock-walled bivy sites; base for Little Mac, East Mac, and West Mac.
waypoints.directions: Drop down the scree or snow on the far side of the notch to the flat gravel benches of camp at about 5,800 ft.

waypoints.name: Loose Rock Below the Summit Block
waypoints.note: Southern Pickets rock is notoriously fractured here; test holds and stagger climbers on the 5.4 pitches to avoid knocking rock onto partners below.
waypoints.directions: From camp, cross the basin to the north and northeast over talus and scree, staying on the McMillan side of the basin rather than crossing the Barrier, to the foot of the southwest arete; expect snow and moats at the base well into summer. Climb the lower arete on class 4 and low fifth-class rock, testing every hold, to the fractured band below the summit block.

waypoints.name: Little Mac Spire
waypoints.note: Approximate — no independently surveyed summit coordinate found for this minor Southern Pickets spire; cross-referenced against neighboring McMillan/Terror group summits and the route's recorded approach track to place it as close to the true high point as possible.
waypoints.directions: Continue up the arete above the loose band on class 4 and low fifth-class rock to the summit.

waypoints.name: Barclay Lake Trailhead (FR-6024)
waypoints.note: FR-6024 (Barclay Creek Road) dead-ends here; self-pay day-use fee ($5) or Northwest Forest Pass required at the kiosk.
