waypoints.directions: Leave US 2 near Baring and follow FR-6024, the Barclay Creek Road, to where it dead-ends at the Barclay Lake trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass or the $5 self-pay day-use fee is required at the kiosk. Barclay Creek runs past the trailhead, so you can top off water here before starting up Barclay Lake Trail #1055 — treat it before drinking.

waypoints.name: Y-shaped creek / gully departure
waypoints.note: Leave the Barclay Lake trail a few hundred feet past the Barclay Creek bridge at this Y-shaped creek fork (not the drainage closer to the lake) to start the south gully scramble.
waypoints.directions: Follow the maintained Barclay Lake Trail #1055 east through old-growth on easy, well-graded tread beside Barclay Creek. The creek mouth you are aiming for has grown in badly; the tell is a faint boot path of piled rocks running a hundred or two hundred feet into the trees to reach the creek bed proper. This is the most commonly missed point on the route, so identify it against a GPS track or a route photo rather than by feel.

waypoints.name: Lower waterfalls (Waterfall 1 & 2)
waypoints.note: First two pour-offs in the gully are bypassed on brushy ledges to the side; footing is loose and slick when wet.
waypoints.directions: From here the drainage is the trail: boulder-hop and scramble straight up the creek bed. The first pour-off is turned on climbers-left on an established boot path; the second is passed by working right toward the cliff band and traversing over the top of the falls. Put helmets on before you start up — the gully is narrow and anything a party above dislodges comes down it.

waypoints.name: Waterfall 3 chockstone crux
waypoints.note: Crux of the route: jammed boulders form a 15-20 ft chimney with small holds on very loose rock over sandy mud; most parties downclimb this same spot on descent.
waypoints.directions: Continue up the gully to where large jammed boulders block it completely. The way through is a Class 3-4 line on climbers-left: a 15-20 ft chimney squeeze on small holds set in loose, sandy rock, with real exposure. Many parties carry a 30m rope for this step even when they intend to downclimb it, and a fixed rap ring has been reported at the top of the falls — treat it as aged gear of unknown condition and back it up with your own natural anchor if you use it.

waypoints.name: Cave feature / gully exit
waypoints.note: A small cave-like rock feature marks where to leave the main gully onto a faint climbers' path through forest and open heather slopes.
waypoints.directions: Above the chockstone the gully eases and opens out into brush and then forest for another 800 ft of gain. Stay in the main drainage the whole way rather than being drawn into side branches, and fix in your mind where you leave it — coming back down into the wrong drainage is the standard descent mistake here.

waypoints.name: Upper alpine meadows/bowl
waypoints.note: Trail fades out in the upper heather meadows; angle climbers' left across talus toward the summit block and final ridge.
waypoints.directions: Pick up the faint climbers' path where it leaves the drainage and follow it up through forest onto open heather, trending climbers-left. It is thin and comes and goes, so treat it as a hint rather than a trail.

waypoints.name: Merchant Peak Summit
waypoints.note: True summit is the northwest high point of the ridge; a lower east peak nearby is commonly mislabeled as Merchant Peak on older maps.
waypoints.directions: Cross the talus out of the bowl and gain the East Ridge, then follow the crest for a final 300 ft or so. The rock here is solid and the scrambling is straightforward Class 3 — a marked change from the loose, sandy ground everywhere below.

waypoints.name: Stuart Lake Trailhead (FR 7601)
waypoints.directions: From US-2 at the western edge of Leavenworth, turn onto Icicle Creek Road and drive 8.4 miles, then turn left onto FS Road 7601 and follow the bumpy dirt road 3.7 miles to the Stuart Lake Trailhead at its end. FS Road 7601 is typically closed November to May. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park, and day climbers fill out the self-issue Enchantment permit at the trailhead.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Lake outlet / north end
waypoints.directions: Follow the Stuart Lake Trail up Mountaineer Creek through forest, crossing on a log bridge at about 1.5 miles. At about 2.25 miles, take the Colchuck Lake Trail where it splits from the Stuart Lake Trail. It crosses Mountaineer Creek again on a log bridge, then climbs steep, rocky tread and a boulder moraine to the lake's outlet. This is the last water.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Balanced Rock summit
waypoints.directions: Follow the trail around the lake to the foot of Aasgard Pass and take the cairned climbers' path about 400 ft up steep talus and heather. Then break climber's left through 15 to 20 minutes of dense slide alder and heather to the gully system below the wall. Loose 3rd and 4th class scrambling leads to the base. Climb the route to the summit.

waypoints.name: Lake Ann Trailhead (Austin Pass)
waypoints.note: Paved lot on SR 542 just below Artist Point; Northwest Forest Pass required, overnight parties sign the trailhead register (no camping permit needed).
waypoints.directions: Drive Mount Baker Highway (SR 542) to its end at the Austin Pass/Artist Point trailhead, a paved lot roughly 58 miles and 1.5-2 hours from Bellingham. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park, and overnight parties sign the wilderness register at the trailhead; no camping permit is needed. The upper highway to Austin Pass typically doesn't open until late June or early July, depending on snowpack, and the trailhead has had weekend-focused access in recent seasons, so check current alerts before planning a start time.

waypoints.name: Swift Creek meadow crossing
waypoints.note: Trail bottoms out through a wildflower meadow alongside upper Swift Creek before climbing again; reliable water but snowfields can bury the crossing into August.
waypoints.directions: From the trailhead, follow Lake Ann Trail #600 as it switchbacks down into the upper Swift Creek basin, about 2.2 miles and 650 ft of descent, to the meadows alongside the creek.

waypoints.name: Swift Creek Trail 607 junction
waypoints.note: Trail drops ~800 ft from the trailhead into the Swift Creek headwaters basin; Swift Creek Trail splits off here, stay on Lake Ann Trail 600.
waypoints.directions: Continue about a quarter mile down the valley to the trail's low point near 3,900 ft, where the Swift Creek Trail splits off down-valley; stay on the Lake Ann Trail.

waypoints.name: 4,900-ft saddle NW of Lake Ann
waypoints.note: Leave the maintained trail here; a boot path heads southwest then south along the ridge toward Peak 5681 — this is the scramble jump-off point.
waypoints.directions: Climb the Lake Ann Trail out of the basin, about 1.5 miles and 950 ft of gain, to the 4,900-ft saddle northwest of Lake Ann. Leave the trail here, before it drops to the lake.

waypoints.name: Ridge steepening / indistinct boot path
waypoints.note: Path contours the east side of the ridge and gets hard to follow above ~5,300 ft; stay high on the ridge crest and watch for cairns rather than dropping onto loose east-facing slopes.
waypoints.directions: From the saddle, take the boot path southwest and then south along the ridge crest to about 5,300 ft, where the ridge steepens and the path becomes hard to follow.

waypoints.name: Peak 5681 (Han Peak/Mount Annette)
waypoints.note: Tree-covered subsidiary summit on the connecting ridge; from here continue west along an up-and-down ridge crest (steeper than it looks on the topo) toward Mount Ann.
waypoints.directions: Follow cairns up through the steeper section until the crest re-forms, then along it to the tree-covered top of Peak 5681. It is not the summit; the ridge continues west.

waypoints.name: Mount Ann summit
waypoints.note: True summit, ~0.5 mi west of Peak 5681 along the ridge; Class 2-3 scrambling on the final pitch with views of Mount Shuksan and Mount Baker.
waypoints.directions: Scramble about half a mile west along the up-and-down ridge crest, steeper than it looks on the map, to the summit; the final bit is class 2-3.

waypoints.name: Obstruction Point Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of Obstruction Point Road (highest road in Olympic NP, gravel, no trailers), 8 mi east of Hurricane Ridge Visitor Center; Grand Pass Trail begins here.
waypoints.directions: Obstruction Point Road is the way in, and it is the highest road in Olympic National Park: from the Hurricane Ridge Visitor Center follow it 8 miles east to its end at the Obstruction Point trailhead, topping out around 6,135 ft. It is narrow, one-lane gravel the whole way and no place for trailers. The road is usually open only from early-to-mid July through mid-October, so it is not a road you can count on before July — confirm it is open before committing to the drive. The Grand Pass Trail starts at the road end, and an online wilderness camping permit plus a bear canister are required for the Cameron Basin camp zone.

waypoints.name: Grand Pass
waypoints.note: Grand Pass Trail crests the divide here between the Grand/Lillian River drainages and Cameron Creek; the descent to the Cameron side is steep and can be dangerously slick in wet weather or lingering snow.
waypoints.directions: From Obstruction Point follow the Grand Pass Trail south along the open crest of Lillian Ridge, descend into Grand Valley and follow the trail up the valley past Moose and Gladys Lakes to Grand Pass, about 6 miles from the trailhead.

waypoints.name: Cameron Creek meadow crossings
waypoints.note: Trail drops off Grand Pass through brushy overgrowth and crosses several unbridged branches of Cameron Creek in a wet meadow; reliable water but the tread is easy to lose in fog or high brush.
waypoints.directions: Drop steeply south off Grand Pass on the Cameron side, a descent that is slick in wet weather or lingering snow, through brushy overgrowth to the wet meadow where the trail crosses several unbridged branches of Cameron Creek. The tread is easy to lose here in fog or high brush.

waypoints.name: Cameron Basin camp
waypoints.note: Established backcountry sites in the upper basin below Cameron Pass along Cameron Creek; bear canister required (no trees to hang food), no campfires above 3,500 ft, and an online wilderness camping permit is mandatory.
waypoints.directions: Continue up along Cameron Creek into the upper basin below Cameron Pass to the established camp sites at about 6,000 ft. A bear canister is required and there are no fires.

waypoints.name: Cameron Pass snow slopes
waypoints.note: Steep snow can persist on the pass into late July or August; ice axe and self-arrest skills recommended, and the climbers' path is frequently obscured under snow here.
waypoints.directions: Continue up the Cameron Pass Trail from the basin to Cameron Pass. Steep snow can cover the climbers' path on the final slopes into late July or August, so carry an ice axe.

waypoints.name: Mount Cameron summit
waypoints.note: True 7,190 ft highpoint of triple-summited Mount Cameron, reached from Cameron Basin/Pass by Class 2 scree and talus along the ridge that rises east from the pass.
waypoints.directions: From Cameron Pass leave the trail and follow the broad ridge crest east and up on Class 1-2 scree and talus. The ridge crosses many false summits, so do not stop at the first high point; the true top is still easy ground, and Class 3-4 steps mean you have passed it and started the traverse toward the Middle Peak.

waypoints.name: Merritt Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Signed spur (FR 657) north off Hwy 2 near milepost 76; no permit required, self-register at the trailhead kiosk.
waypoints.directions: From US-2 near milepost 76, about 11.5 miles east of Stevens Pass or 24 miles west of Leavenworth, turn north onto the signed spur for Forest Road 657. The road is rough and high clearance is recommended; drive 1.5 miles to the Merritt Lake Trailhead at about 3,050 feet. No permit is required, but self-register at the trailhead kiosk before you start hiking.

waypoints.name: Merritt Lake
waypoints.note: Top of the switchbacking Merritt Lake Trail; established campsites and a privy here, and the last dependable water before the ridge.
waypoints.directions: Hike the Merritt Lake Trail as it switchbacks up through forest for about 2.5 miles to Merritt Lake, where there are established campsites, a privy, and the last dependable water before the ridge.

waypoints.name: Boot path split for Mastiff
waypoints.note: About a mile north on the Nason Ridge Trail past the Merritt Lake junction, an unsigned boot path breaks off uphill toward Mastiff's south slopes — easy to walk past if you're not watching for it.
waypoints.directions: Continue past the lake junction onto the Nason Ridge Trail and follow it north about a mile, watching for an unsigned boot path breaking off uphill toward the peak's south slopes. There is no cairn, post or blaze; if the trail starts losing height toward Lost Lake, you have passed the turn and should come back.

waypoints.name: South-slope heather/talus
waypoints.note: Above treeline the boot path fades into open heather and loose talus with no maintained tread and no water; fog or whiteout makes relocating the descent path difficult.
waypoints.directions: Follow the boot path steeply uphill through forest. Above treeline it fades into open heather and loose talus with no maintained tread and no water, so note landmarks for the descent, especially in fog.

waypoints.name: Mount Mastiff summit
waypoints.note: True summit, third-highest point on Nason Ridge; open views north to Lake Wenatchee and west along the connecting ridge/saddle to Mount Howard, a common combined objective.
waypoints.directions: Gain the ridge and climb it until it turns into a rocky, jagged crest. Follow the moat between rock and snow just to the left, stepping up onto the rock to cross ledges, wrap the big rock tower on its right side close to its base, then scramble dirt and ledges to a knoll and a final snowfield. The summit is broad and flat; the register sits off to the south of the flat area rather than on the high point.

waypoints.name: Hoh River Trailhead (Hoh Rain Forest Visitor Center)
waypoints.note: Hoh Rain Forest Visitor Center trailhead; shared start for multiple Mount Olympus routes.
waypoints.directions: From US 101 about 13 miles south of Forks, turn east on Upper Hoh Road and drive about 18 miles to the road end at the Hoh Rain Forest Visitor Center, about 578 ft. A park entrance pass is required, and overnight trips need an Olympic National Park wilderness permit booked in advance; the Hoh is a quota area.

waypoints.name: Lewis Meadows Camp, Hoh River trail
Elk Lake Camp, Hoh River trail
Glacier Meadows — the standard Blue Glacier base camp
Snow Dome high camp
waypoints.directions: Follow the Hoh River Trail about 17.5 miles to Glacier Meadows at about 4,300 ft, crossing the ladder and fixed rope at the washout just below the meadows. Take the way trail onto the lateral moraine crest, drop onto the Blue Glacier and rope up, then climb about 2 miles of glacier to Snow Dome.

waypoints.name: West Ridge moat (gain ridge)
waypoints.directions: Cross the Blue Glacier to the southwest, keeping Crystal Pass, Five Fingers Ridge and the West Peak in view as references, to the moat at the ridge's lowest point near 7,260 ft. If you find yourself climbing toward Crystal Pass, you have drifted onto the standard route.

waypoints.name: Mount Olympus (West Peak)
waypoints.directions: Cross the moat and climb about 600 ft of ridge in roughly seven pitches, never harder than 5.4, staying high but slightly south of the loose crest and using shallow gullies, to the base of the summit block, then climb the roughly 100-ft block to the top.

waypoints.name: White Salmon Lodge road gate (Mount Baker Highway hairpin)
waypoints.directions: From Glacier, drive the Mount Baker Highway (SR-542) east about 18 miles to the hairpin switchback at roughly 3,500 ft, below the ski area, and park in the small pull-off at the gated White Salmon Road (FS 3075). Parking is very limited and is not allowed on the highway shoulder; do not block the gate. No parking pass is required.

waypoints.name: White Salmon Glacier toe
waypoints.note: Glacier travel begins where the road/approach ends.
waypoints.directions: Walk around the gate and follow the old road past the White Salmon Lodge site for about a mile to where it ends at an old clearcut. With good snow cover, descend to White Salmon Creek and follow the valley up to the glacier's toe; without it, hold your height through the clearcut and contour, losing elevation only to get around rock bands and stream crossings, to stay out of the slide alder in the valley bottom.

waypoints.name: White Salmon Glacier
waypoints.directions: Rope up and climb the White Salmon Glacier, weaving between rock outcrops and crevasses. The basin below sits under the active Hanging Glacier, whose avalanches can sweep it, so move through early and don't linger.

waypoints.name: Winnie's Slide
waypoints.note: 150-200 ft step of steep 40-45° snow/ice onto the Upper Curtis Glacier; schrund can be tricky late season.
waypoints.directions: Continue up the glacier among the outcrops to the foot of Winnie's Slide at about 6,800 ft, the only abrupt steepening on this side of the mountain.

waypoints.name: Hell's Highway
waypoints.note: Snow chute connecting to the west edge of the Sulphide Glacier.
waypoints.directions: Climb Winnie's Slide, about 150-200 ft of 40-45 degree snow that can be hard snow or ice late season, onto the Upper Curtis Glacier. Cross the Upper Curtis southward: it starts steep, eases, then loses height to the base of Hell's Highway. Keep the rope tight as crevasses open through the summer.

waypoints.name: Mount Shuksan
waypoints.directions: Climb Hell's Highway, a short chute of steep snow or alpine ice between rock cliffs, watching for a moat where snow meets rock, onto the upper west edge of the Sulphide Glacier. Follow the Sulphide northeast to the foot of the summit pyramid and finish by the central gully on its south face (3rd-4th class) or the West Ridge (4th class).

waypoints.name: Goodell Creek Group Camp Trailhead
waypoints.note: Off SR-20 near Newhalem; park at Upper Goodell Creek Group Camp and pick up the old roadbed/climbers' path paralleling Goodell Creek — North Cascades NP wilderness permit required for overnight camping.
waypoints.directions: Turn north off Highway 20 directly across from Newhalem Campground onto the unpaved Goodell Creek Road and follow it to the Upper Goodell Creek Group Camp trailhead, at about 600 feet. Park at the group camp and pick up the old roadbed and climbers' path paralleling Goodell Creek. A North Cascades National Park wilderness permit is required for overnight camping; pick it up in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Info Center, since this zone cannot be reserved in advance.

waypoints.name: Terror Basin path turnoff (cairn)
waypoints.note: Small rock cairns and a few logs laid across the old roadbed mark the unsigned turnoff onto the Terror Basin climbers' path; a small campsite sits here, easy to walk past in fog.
waypoints.directions: Follow the old abandoned roadbed and boot path northeast along Goodell Creek on a gentle grade to a stone cairn and arrow near 1,700 ft that marks the unsigned start of the Terror Basin climbers' path. A small campsite sits here, and the spot is easy to walk past in fog.

waypoints.name: Treeline stream break (~5,000')
waypoints.note: Last reliable running water before the climb steepens above treeline; parties report long dry stretches on the ridge above here in late summer.
waypoints.directions: Take the hard right at the cairn rather than continuing straight on the fainter track along Terror Creek, and climb the steep, well-beaten Terror Basin boot path directly up through old-growth forest, over 3,000 ft in about 1.5 miles, until it breaks out above treeline around 5,000 ft.

waypoints.name: ~6,200' notch above Terror Basin
waypoints.note: Climbers' path tops out at heather benches and a rock notch on the spur ridge overlooking Terror Basin — the col to descend into camp; often holds moderate snow into midsummer.
waypoints.directions: Above the trees, make a rising traverse across heather benches, slabs and early-season snowfields to the broad saddle and rock notch near 6,200 ft overlooking Terror Basin. Expect loose rock and some route-finding on the upper slabs.

waypoints.name: Terror Basin bivy
waypoints.note: Small flat gravelly basin just below the notch with running water; the zone takes only 6 parties a night and cannot be reserved, so be at Marblemount early in peak season.
waypoints.directions: Drop about 400 ft beyond the saddle into the gravelly, flower-filled basin at about 5,800 ft, where several small streams give reliable water.

waypoints.name: 5.7 crux chimney/dihedral
waypoints.note: Exposed technical crux on the right (west) rib of the north face where the route breaks from Class 3-4 scrambling into a short 5.7 chimney/dihedral before the summit snow finger.
waypoints.directions: Cross the Barrier into Crescent Creek Basin, then cross the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col and descend the crevassed Mustard Glacier into McMillan Cirque to the foot of the face. Start just left of the snowpatch, climb long rightward-traversing third-class ground onto the right (west) rib, follow dihedrals to the darkening west crest, then move back left onto the face to the chimney.

waypoints.name: Mount Terror summit
waypoints.note: True summit of the Southern Pickets' highest peak; standard descent goes back over the top and down the West Ridge gully into Crescent Creek Basin rather than reversing the face.
waypoints.directions: Above the chimney, follow the long snow finger up the upper face, scramble the wildly exposed crest, and traverse around a small tower to the notch between the false and true summits. Take the false summit on an exposed easy fifth-class hand traverse, downclimb it, and make the short climb to the true summit.

waypoints.name: Hoh River Trailhead (Hoh Rain Forest Visitor Center)
waypoints.note: Overnight wilderness permits must be reserved in advance — none are issued at the trailhead kiosk by the visitor center; NPS entrance fee applies.
waypoints.directions: From Forks, drive south on US 101 about 13 miles and turn east onto Upper Hoh Road. Follow it about 18 miles to its end at the Hoh Rain Forest Visitor Center, where the Hoh River Trail begins. An Olympic National Park entrance pass is required, and overnight wilderness permits must be reserved in advance.

waypoints.name: Five Mile Island
waypoints.note: Trail stays nearly flat along the Hoh River through old-growth rainforest with frequent side-creek water access.

waypoints.name: Elk Lake camp
waypoints.note: Reservable backcountry camp with privy and bear wire; last reliable easy water before the trail climbs steeply to Glacier Meadows.

waypoints.name: Glacier Meadows high camp
waypoints.note: Old ranger-station camp near timberline; no camping is permitted between here and the Blue Glacier moraine.

waypoints.name: Top of Blue Glacier lateral moraine
waypoints.note: Way trail tops the moraine; the scree descent onto the ice is steep, loose, and washed out — watch for rockfall while dropping onto the glacier.

waypoints.name: Blue Glacier crossing to Snow Dome
waypoints.note: Rope up here — the glacier is riddled with crevasses and icefall; Snow Dome is the broad basin where the Olympus (east) and Mount Tom/White-Hubert Glacier (west) lines diverge.

waypoints.name: White/Hubert Glacier traverse to Tom-Olympus col
waypoints.note: Continue roped travel across the crevassed White/Hubert Glacier along the base of the Olympus massif to gain the col below Mount Tom.

waypoints.name: Mount Tom summit
waypoints.note: Class 3-4 scramble up from the col; westernmost 7,000+ ft summit in the contiguous US, with the White Glacier visible falling away below.

removed.wp: Top of Blue Glacier lateral moraine
Blue Glacier crossing to Snow Dome

waypoints.name: Mount Washington Trailhead (FR-2419)
waypoints.note: End of FR-2419 off North Lake Cushman Road/FR 24; Northwest Forest Pass required to park, no wilderness permit needed.
waypoints.directions: From the T-intersection at the end of North Lake Cushman Road, turn right onto FS Road 24 and continue about 1.5 miles, then turn left onto FS Road 2419 and follow it up the Big Creek drainage for roughly 6.6 miles to its end at a small trailhead and parking area near 3,026 ft. Display a Northwest Forest Pass; no wilderness permit is needed.

waypoints.name: Climbers' path / rock gullies
waypoints.note: The boot path turns into a climbers' path up steep, narrow rock gullies studded with tree roots — hand-over-hand in spots.
waypoints.directions: From the road-end parking, follow the boot path into the forest. Within a few hundred yards it steepens into narrow rock gullies laced with tree roots, climbed hand over hand in places.

waypoints.name: Lower meadow
waypoints.note: Grade eases briefly in an open meadow where the ridgeline and neighboring Mount Ellinor come into view.
waypoints.directions: Climb the rooty gullies directly up through the timber until the grade eases at an open meadow bench around 3,800 ft, where the ridgeline and Mount Ellinor come into view.

waypoints.name: Upper talus/scree field
waypoints.note: Route climbs a broad talus and scree slope above the meadow; footing is loose, watch for rockfall from parties above.
waypoints.directions: Above the meadow, climb onto the broad scree and talus slopes and keep to the climber's-left side of the large, loose rocky gully. Spread the party out so nobody knocks rock onto those below.

waypoints.name: 5,600' ramp at the headwall
waypoints.note: Crux route-finding point: path swings west onto a ramp that hugs the headwall briefly, then ducks back through trees.
waypoints.directions: Continue up the climber's-left side of the gully to about 5,600 ft, where the path swings west onto a ramp along the base of the headwall.

waypoints.name: South saddle
waypoints.note: Known bivy site on the saddle; first spot on the climb where the true summit becomes visible.
waypoints.directions: Follow the ramp briefly along the headwall, duck back through the trees, and wind above the gully onto the southern ridgeline at the saddle, about 5,950 ft, the first spot where the true summit comes into view.

waypoints.name: The Catwalk
waypoints.note: Exposed knife-edge ledge crux move on the final ridge; helmet recommended, some parties rig a handline here.
waypoints.directions: From the saddle, follow the faint goat trail along the ridge crest toward the summit to the Catwalk, where the tread narrows to a boot-width with exposure on both sides. Move one at a time.

waypoints.name: Mount Washington summit
waypoints.note: True summit (6,255'); exposed east-facing ridge on the final approach, summit register present.
waypoints.directions: Past the Catwalk, continue along the ridge to the scree field below the false summit, take the goat trail up its climber's-right edge to a stone wind shelter on the ridge, then scramble the final short Class 3-4 step to the true summit.

waypoints.name: Watson Lakes Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FS Rd 1107022; Northwest Forest Pass or digital day-use pass required, vault toilet but no potable water on site.
waypoints.directions: Park at the Watson Lakes Trailhead at the end of FS Road 1107, about 4,300 ft, reached via Baker Lake Road (FS-11) and then FS-1106 around Baker Lake. FS 1107 has been closed at a washout near milepost 3.8, short of the trailhead; check its status before you go. A Northwest Forest Pass or digital day-use pass is required to park here. There is a vault toilet at the trailhead but no potable water on site, and the first reliable water is at the Watson Lakes themselves. The Anderson-Watson Lakes Trail #611 leaves straight from the lot into the woods.

waypoints.name: Anderson Butte Trail 611.1 junction
waypoints.note: Trail 611 winds gently through forest to a meadow junction; stay right/straight on 611 toward Anderson-Watson Lakes rather than climbing left to the old Anderson Butte lookout site.
waypoints.directions: Follow the Anderson-Watson Lakes Trail #611 from the lot through forest for about a mile to the meadow junction with the Anderson Butte Trail #611.1.

waypoints.name: Anderson/Watson Lakes fork
waypoints.note: Second junction at ~4,700 ft: right fork drops 0.5 mi to lower Anderson Lake, left fork climbs 0.5 mi to the saddle (Watson Pass) — take the left/south fork for Mount Watson.
waypoints.directions: Stay right on Trail #611 toward the lakes rather than climbing left toward the old Anderson Butte lookout site, and continue to the next junction at about 4,700 ft.

waypoints.name: Saddle above Watson Lakes
waypoints.note: The trail climbs about half a mile from the fork to this saddle at the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness boundary, then continues as maintained trail down to the Watson Lakes, where the scramble route leaves the tread. A boot path also heads south from here along the ridge toward Upper Anderson Lakes, a longer alternative way onto the north side of the peak.
waypoints.directions: Take the left fork, which climbs about half a mile to a small saddle at the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness boundary; the right fork drops to lower Anderson Lake.

waypoints.name: Watson Lakes basin
waypoints.note: The trail descends off the saddle into the Watson Lakes basin; the lower (farther) lake is larger with clear blue water and is the recommended spot to filter water and camp nearby.
waypoints.directions: Follow the trail down off the saddle to the Watson Lakes at about 4,400 ft. The maintained trail ends here, and the lakes are the last reliable water.

waypoints.name: Camp on slopes below Mount Watson (~5,400 ft)
waypoints.note: Established bivy sites on open slopes beneath the peak with views of Mt Baker and Mt Shuksan; last practical camp before the summit push.
waypoints.directions: Leave the tread at the lakes and follow the open, cairned climbers' route up talus, heather and, into summer, snow on the slopes below the peak to the bivy sites around 5,400 ft.

waypoints.name: Moat / snow bridge below summit gullies
waypoints.note: In late season the west gully develops a large moat and an unstable snow bridge — parties have had to reroute to the more stable east gully instead.
waypoints.directions: This is the gully to stay out of. Late in the season the west gully develops a large moat and an unstable snow bridge; take the widest gully east of the peak to the saddle at about 5,900 ft instead.

waypoints.name: Mount Watson summit
waypoints.note: Short, steep, tightly-treed Class 3 scramble gains an airy ~30 ft summit ridge with real exposure on both sides; a fixed hand-line is commonly used here, and descent reverses the same route down the east gully.
waypoints.directions: Climb the widest gully east of the peak to the saddle at about 5,900 ft, avoiding the west gully. From the saddle, head west along the south side of the ridge into the basin below the summit block, cross it to the heather-and-dirt gully on the block's south side, squeeze through the trees partway up, then scramble the short block and the narrow, exposed 30 ft ridge to the top.

waypoints.name: Hoh River Trailhead (Hoh Rain Forest Visitor Center)
waypoints.note: Start of Hoh River Trail, the standard ~17.3 mi approach to Glacier Meadows and Blue Glacier for all Olympus summit routes.
waypoints.directions: From Forks, drive south on US 101 about 13 miles and turn east onto the Upper Hoh Road. Follow it about 18 miles to its end at the Hoh Rain Forest Visitor Center, where the Hoh River Trail begins. An Olympic National Park entrance pass is required, and overnight trips need a wilderness camping permit.

waypoints.name: Lewis Meadows Camp, Hoh River trail
Elk Lake Camp, Hoh River trail
Glacier Meadows
waypoints.note: High camp for the traverse, with shelters and an outhouse; the way path to the Blue Glacier moraine starts here.
waypoints.directions: Follow the Hoh River Trail about 17.4 miles up the valley, past Lewis Meadow and Elk Lake, to the Glacier Meadows camp.

waypoints.name: Snow Dome
waypoints.note: Broad snow summit on the upper Blue Glacier where the line turns toward Crystal Pass.
waypoints.directions: Take the way path onto the crest of the lateral moraine and drop onto the Blue Glacier. Rope up, cross the lower glacier and climb through the rock islands to Snow Dome.

waypoints.name: West Peak
waypoints.directions: Stay roped over Crystal Pass, traverse below Five Fingers Ridge and over the false summit, then climb the short snow slope to the platform below the 80 ft summit tower and climb the tower to the West Peak.

waypoints.name: Middle Peak
waypoints.note: Second summit of the traverse; loose Class 3-4 rock.
waypoints.directions: Descend from the West Peak to the saddle between the West and Middle Peaks, with careful route-finding and downclimbing, then scramble loose Class 3-4 rock to the Middle Peak.

waypoints.name: East Peak
waypoints.note: Last summit of the traverse; the usual exit descends toward Glacier Pass and the Blue Glacier.
waypoints.directions: Traverse the narrow ridge east from the Middle Peak, Class 3-4 with exposure on both sides, to the East Peak.

waypoints.name: North Fork Entiat Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR 5606; self-issue Northwest Forest Pass/day-use fee kiosk at the lot, day-use only with no camping at the TH itself.
waypoints.directions: From US 97A in Entiat, turn onto Entiat River Road (County Road 19) at the bridge and drive about 32 miles up the valley; it becomes FS Road 51 along the way. Turn onto FS Road 5606 and follow it about 3 miles to the road end. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park, and a free self-issued Glacier Peak Wilderness permit is available at the trailhead.

waypoints.name: Fern Lake Trail (#1436) junction
waypoints.note: Trail #1437 tops a switchbacking climb away from the river here where the short Fern Lake spur splits off; stay on #1437 toward the Pyramid Mtn Trail rather than detouring to the lake.
waypoints.directions: Trail #1437 runs up the North Fork Entiat valley for about six miles, mostly gentle beside the river before switchbacks lift you away from it. The tread carries a reputation for blowdown, so budget time for it even when reports say it is clear.

waypoints.name: Pyramid Mountain Trail (#1433) junction camp
waypoints.note: Flat clearing where Trail #1437 meets the Pyramid Mtn Trail; a nearby log/plank crossing has been reported to flex badly in high water and is the usual base camp before heading off-trail toward Saska Pass.
waypoints.directions: Roughly two and a half miles on from the Fern Lake spur, staying on #1437. Fill water at the crossing here: the drainages between this junction and the pass are seasonal and are often dry.

waypoints.name: Saska Pass
waypoints.note: Gain the pass off-trail via a steep dry streambed and a loose scree headwall; it marks the crest between the Emerald Peak basin and the Snow Brushy Creek burn drainage leading to Pinnacle's north side.
waypoints.directions: Leave the tread before it starts traversing toward the pass and climb the drainage directly; the traverse sidehills across scree and is slower and more tiring than going straight up. The headwall above the bench is loose enough to be worth a helmet, and it is worse for anyone climbing below you.

waypoints.name: Snow Brushy Creek burn-zone crossing
waypoints.note: Descend roughly 1,500 ft off the pass into the 2006/2015-era burn; ash-covered slopes and heavy standing/fallen burnt snags erase the tread, so carry a GPS track rather than relying on cairns.
waypoints.directions: Head straight down the far side of the pass rather than hunting for tread, because none survives here. The burn is open enough that the descent goes quickly, but every foot of it has to be regained on the way home, and the far bank climbs steeply straight out of the creek.

waypoints.name: Basin below Pinnacle's summit block
waypoints.note: Exit the burn into open larch basins on the peak's north side, then climb loose scree to a bench that sets up the final class 2-3 ridge traverse to the summit.
waypoints.directions: A steep and unrelenting climb of around 1,900 feet out of the creek: poor scree low down where the burn ends, easing as the ground opens higher up. This leg and the reclimb of the pass afterwards are what make the day long, not any difficulty on the peak itself.

waypoints.name: Pinnacle Mountain
waypoints.note: True summit (8,400 ft), first climbed 1948 by Dwight Watson and Ken Fleming; the standard finish is class 3 scrambling up the south-slope talus, which doubles as the descent line.
waypoints.directions: Follow the crest on from the bench, keeping to its west side where the scrambling stays easiest. The rock here is noticeably more solid than the scree below, but it is still a hands-on class 3 finish rather than a walk-up.

waypoints.name: Stuart Lake Trailhead (FR 7601)
waypoints.directions: From US 2 at the west end of Leavenworth, turn onto Icicle Road and drive about 8.5 miles, then turn left onto FR 7601 (Eightmile Road) and follow it about 4 miles to its end at the Stuart Lake Trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park, plus a free self-issued Enchantment day-use permit at the trailhead. FR 7601 is gated closed from late fall through spring.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Lake outlet / north end
waypoints.directions: Hike the Stuart Lake Trail #1599 up Mountaineer Creek, crossing it on a log bridge at about 1.5 miles, and take the left fork onto the Colchuck Lake Trail at the junction. Climb the final boulder moraine to the lake's outlet at its north end, about 4 miles and 2,300 ft from the car. Fill water here.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Balanced Rock summit
waypoints.directions: Follow the trail counter-clockwise around the lake to its south end and onto the cairned Aasgard Pass climbers' trail. At about 400 ft above the lake, cut climber's left through dense slide alder and heather into the gully below the west face and scramble loose 3rd and 4th class ground to the base, then climb the route's five pitches to the summit ridge.

waypoints.name: Boston Basin Trailhead (Cascade River Road pullout)
waypoints.note: Unmarked pullout at mile ~22 of Cascade River Road opposite Johannesburg Mountain, room for 6-8 cars; self-issue wilderness permit and Northwest Forest Pass required.
waypoints.directions: The Boston Basin start is an unmarked climbers' pullout on Cascade River Road, about 21.7 miles from Marblemount at roughly 3,200-3,300 ft, sitting opposite Johannesburg Mountain. There is no trailhead sign of any kind, so watch your odometer rather than looking for signage — it is easy to drive straight past. The pullout holds six to eight cars and you need a Northwest Forest Pass to park. Camping in Boston Basin needs a North Cascades wilderness permit picked up in person at Marblemount, and the popular sites fill fast in the early-access lottery for peak summer weekends.

waypoints.name: Creek crossings through old-growth forest
waypoints.note: Climbers' path follows an old mining road then crosses several small streams in old-growth timber before switchbacking to treeline; reliable water but poorly marked in low light.
waypoints.directions: Walk the old mine roadbed about three quarters of a mile to a mile with almost no gain, past the derelict mine site, and watch for the cairned and flagged climbers' trail leaving the roadbed sharply to the right and going straight up; it is easy to walk past. The steep path switchbacks through forest and a brushy old slide path with deadfall to a series of small stream crossings in old-growth timber, the last reliable water before camp.

waypoints.name: Boston Basin low camp
waypoints.note: Designated moraine campsite with composting toilet at treeline; most parties continue higher for a shorter summit day.
waypoints.directions: Keep climbing the steep, switchbacking climbers' path above the streams to treeline at about 5,300 ft, where the low camp sits on heather benches and moraine.

waypoints.name: Boston Basin high camp
waypoints.note: Upper hardened camp on slabs/grass below Sharkfin Tower, closer to the Quien Sabe Glacier; the informal camps below Sharkfin are on this bench.
waypoints.directions: Continue up the path above the low camp toward Sharkfin Tower to the upper camps on the bench of slabs and grass at about 6,200-6,400 ft.

waypoints.name: Glacier rope-up point beneath Sharkfin Tower
waypoints.note: Where the boot path meets continuous snow on the Quien Sabe Glacier's lower-angle (north/left) side; rope up for crevasses here.
waypoints.directions: From high camp, stay on climber's left and walk moraine and slabs toward the left side of Sharkfin Tower to the toe of the Quien Sabe Glacier. Rope up where the boot path meets continuous snow, around 6,700 ft.

waypoints.name: Bergschrund crossing
waypoints.note: Narrow snow bridge crosses above and left of the bergschrund late-season; crevasses widen through August-September and the crossing point shifts year to year.
waypoints.directions: Make a rising traverse under the cliffs below Sharkfin Tower onto the flatter part of the glacier, then pick a line up the steeper section between crevasses; the left-hand and more direct lines merge partway up. Cross near 7,600 ft on a snow bridge above and left of the bergschrund; the crossing point shifts from year to year.

waypoints.name: Boston-Sahale Col
waypoints.note: Top of the glacier traverse beneath the Sharkfin face; gains the col between Sahale and Boston Peak before the final scramble.
waypoints.directions: Climb the upper glacier to a second crossing near 8,100 ft, where large open crevasses flank the route late in the season. Later in summer the usual line goes right around the end of the bergschrund, then cuts back up and left to the Boston-Sahale col, the only low saddle at the top of the glacier.

waypoints.name: Sahale Mountain summit
waypoints.note: Short, exposed 3rd/4th-class scramble up the summit block from the col; the true summit block has fixed anchors used by many parties to rappel back to the col.
waypoints.directions: From the col, traverse right (south) across a short but exposed snow slope with a rocky step, crampons and axe on and well back from any cornice, to the base of the summit block. Finish with about 60-70 ft of very exposed, loose Class 3 with 4th-class moves to the summit.

waypoints.name: Stuart Lake Trailhead (FR 7601)
waypoints.directions: From US 2 at the west end of Leavenworth, turn onto Icicle Road and drive about 8.5 miles, then turn left onto FR 7601 (Eightmile Road) and follow it about 4 miles to its end at the Stuart Lake Trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park, plus a free self-issued Enchantment day-use permit at the trailhead. FR 7601 is gated closed from late fall through spring.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Lake outlet / north end
waypoints.directions: Hike the Stuart Lake Trail #1599 up Mountaineer Creek, crossing it on a log bridge at about 1.5 miles, and take the left fork onto the Colchuck Lake Trail at the junction. Climb the final boulder moraine to the lake's outlet at its north end, about 4 miles and 2,300 ft from the car. Fill water here.

waypoints.name: Base of Scarface (gully left of the West Face)
waypoints.note: The route starts in the gully just left of the West Face route's start. The ground here is very loose and exposed; keep the party spread out.
waypoints.directions: Follow the trail counter-clockwise around the lake to its south end and onto the cairned Aasgard Pass climbers' trail. At about 400 ft above the lake, cut climber's left through dense slide alder and heather (15-20 minutes) to the gully system below the west face; the start is the gully just left of the West Face route.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Balanced Rock summit
waypoints.directions: Climb the route's six pitches to the summit ridge.

waypoints.name: SR-20 Burgundy Col pullout (MP 165)
waypoints.note: Roadside pullout on the North Cascades Highway, first pullout past the Cutthroat Creek trailhead turnout, ~4 mi east of Washington Pass; no parking pass is needed here.
waypoints.directions: Park at the broad pullout on SR-20 near milepost 165-166, about 4 miles east of Washington Pass — it's the first pullout past the Cutthroat Creek trailhead turnout, marked by a sign pointing toward Silver Star Mountain. No parking pass is needed there. This section of Highway 20 is closed by WSDOT over the winter and typically reopens in mid-spring depending on snowpack, so check road status before planning the trip.

waypoints.name: Early Winters Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Drop down the embankment off the highway and cross on logs — last easy, reliable water until the Bench or Col trickles.

waypoints.name: Larch bench camp ("the Bench")
waypoints.note: Flat larch-shaded bench reached via the climber's trail on the timbered rib left of Burgundy Creek; a seasonal trickle nearby dries up by late summer.

waypoints.name: Burgundy Creek bench camp — west side
Burgundy Col
waypoints.note: Gain the col via the gully above the Bench, staying left; 3-4 exposed bivy sites here and the last snowmelt trickle before the glacier.

waypoints.name: Steep snow drop onto glacier's north flank
waypoints.note: Downclimb steep snow off the col, rope up, and traverse below Burgundy Spire's loose rock slabs — rockfall and, late season, open crevasses.

waypoints.name: Silver Star Glacier saddle
waypoints.note: Top of the Silver Star Glacier at the saddle between the west and east summits; steepens noticeably in the last pitch, crampons/axe mandatory.

waypoints.name: Silver Star Mountain (East Summit)
waypoints.note: True summit is the east peak reached by a short 4th-class scramble off the saddle; Wine Spires ridge visible to the north.

waypoints.name: Alpental / Snow Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Park near the covered bridge at the Alpental Ski Area (I-90 Exit 52); Northwest Forest Pass required at the kiosk.
waypoints.directions: Take I-90 to Exit 52, then follow Alpental Road to its end and park in the Alpental lot near the covered bridge at the ski area, around 3,100 to 3,120 feet. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the trailhead kiosk.

waypoints.name: Unsigned boot path split
waypoints.note: Unmarked climbers' path splits off the signed Snow Lake trail about 50 ft downhill into slide alder - easy to walk past if not watching for it.

waypoints.name: Boulder field, right branch to ridge
waypoints.note: Boot path opens into a boulder field around 4,250 ft; take the (signed) right branch here to climb toward the ridge - straight/left trends toward Guye Peak and Cave Ridge instead.

waypoints.name: Loose talus/scree slope
waypoints.note: Steep, loose talus and scree above the boulder field on the southwest slopes - unstable footing and rockfall risk onto anyone below.

waypoints.name: Ridge tarn
waypoints.note: Small tarn passed just after turning right onto the summit ridge; seasonal snowmelt pool, not a dependable late-season water source.

waypoints.name: Exposed summit-ridge scramble
waypoints.note: Short, exposed Class 3 section on the final summit ridge with loose rock and real fall consequence - the crux of the standard route.

waypoints.name: Snoqualmie Mountain summit
waypoints.note: Trail-accessible summit; a rugged pinnacle about 550 horizontal ft to the east was resurveyed in 2023 as roughly 3 ft higher but requires harder scrambling to tag.

waypoints.name: Artist Point Trailhead / Parking Lot
waypoints.directions: From I-5 Exit 255 in Bellingham, follow SR 542, the Mount Baker Highway, east through Glacier and past the Mt. Baker Ski Area and Heather Meadows to the road's end at the Artist Point parking lot, about 5,100 ft. The last stretch opens only once the snow is cleared, usually in summer. A Northwest Forest Pass or day-use fee is required to park.

waypoints.name: Table Mountain Summit
waypoints.directions: From the northwest corner of the lot, opposite the vault toilets, take Table Mountain Trail #681 up the tight switchbacks cut into the southeast-face cliff band, about 400 ft of exposed tread, onto the flat plateau. Follow the main path west-northwest along the south rim, ignoring the braided use-trails, about 1.4 miles in all to the high point.

waypoints.name: Twin Lakes Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of the rough, high-clearance-only FS-3065 spur past the Yellow Aster Butte/Tomyhoi trailhead; Northwest Forest Pass required and self-issue Mt. Baker Wilderness permit at the kiosk.
waypoints.directions: From Glacier, drive east on SR 542 (Mt. Baker Highway) about 12 miles to the WSDOT Shuksan maintenance facility and turn onto Twin Lakes Road (FS-3065). The first 4.5 miles are passenger-car friendly, reaching the Yellow Aster Butte/Tomyhoi Lake trailhead; beyond that the road narrows, turns rocky, and is not maintained for passenger vehicles, so high-clearance is recommended and 4WD helps for the final two miles to the road's end at Twin Lakes, 6.5 miles total from the highway. The road is often snow-covered or rough into early summer, with conditions typically best in August and September; if the upper stretch is washed out, park instead at the Yellow Aster Butte/Tomyhoi Lake trailhead, which adds roughly 4 miles round trip and 1,500 feet of gain to the day. A Northwest Forest Pass is required, along with a self-issue Mount Baker Wilderness permit at the kiosk.

waypoints.name: Isthmus between the Twin Lakes
waypoints.note: Established primitive camp on the strip of ground between the two lakes; reliable water from both lakes but treat before drinking (basin often holds snow into July).
waypoints.directions: The isthmus camp sits on the strip of ground between the two Twin Lakes, a few minutes' walk from the road end.

waypoints.name: High Pass Trail split off Winchester Mountain Trail
waypoints.note: Bear right onto High Pass Trail 676 here; the left fork climbs 1,300 ft to the Winchester Mountain fire lookout.
waypoints.directions: Start up the Winchester Mountain Trail #685 from between the lakes and, a short way up, bear right at the signed junction onto High Pass Trail #676; the left fork climbs to the Winchester lookout.

waypoints.name: Avalanche chute / Low Pass traverse below Winchester
waypoints.note: Trail drops about 300 ft to cross a steep chute below Winchester Mountain; snow lingers here into August and requires an ice axe and solid snow-travel skills before then.
waypoints.directions: Follow High Pass Trail #676 as it traverses below Winchester Mountain, dropping about 300 ft to cross a steep avalanche chute that can hold snow into August.

waypoints.name: High Pass
waypoints.note: Broad saddle on the ridge crest; a faint boot path and cairns continue north toward Mt. Larrabee and the Pleiades ridge, while the old Gargett Mine tailings are visible in the basin below to the north.
waypoints.directions: Continue on the trail past the chute, climbing over Low Pass and on to High Pass, the broad saddle on the ridge crest.

waypoints.name: Notch between the first and second Pleiades peaks
waypoints.note: Exposed 4th-class notch and knife-edge rock traverse linking the Pleiades summits on notoriously loose, 'garbage' rock; helmet essential and expect route-finding.
waypoints.directions: Leave the trail and climb the scree or snow slope NNE about 400-500 ft to the col in Larrabee's south arm. Descend slightly from the col, traverse the basin about half a mile, then climb the loose, narrow gully to the notch between the first and second Pleiades.

waypoints.name: The Pleiades (Peak 3, high point)
waypoints.note: True/high summit of the four-peak Pleiades group, reached via 3rd/4th-class gully and ridge scrambling continuing from High Pass along Mt. Larrabee's east ridge extension.
waypoints.directions: From the notch, scramble up to the goat ledge and traverse it east; a little over halfway along, leave the ledge and scramble loose 3rd/4th-class rock to the third Pleiad, the high point of the group.

removed.wp: High Pass Trail split off Winchester Mountain Trail

waypoints.name: Goodell Creek / Upper Goodell Group Camp trailhead (SR-20, Newhalem)
waypoints.note: Standard cross-country-zone access for Southern Pickets objectives (Terror Basin/Crescent Creek Basin);
waypoints.directions: Drive SR-20 east to Newhalem. Just after crossing Goodell Creek, take the first left onto a small road and turn immediately left at the T, then take the right branch uphill to the Upper Goodell Creek Group Camp; the climbers' path starts just back down the road from the camp. An overnight North Cascades wilderness permit, walk-up only from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, is required to camp in Terror or Crescent Creek basins.

waypoints.name: Goodell Creek Branch Crossings
waypoints.note: Climbers' path fords two branches of Goodell Creek on the old roadbed; can run high and fast during snowmelt.
waypoints.directions: Follow the unmaintained climbers' path up the old roadbed along Goodell Creek; about 1.5 miles in it fords two branches of the creek, which can run high and fast during snowmelt.

waypoints.name: Terror Creek Basin Cairn Turnoff
waypoints.note: A stone cairn marks where the boot path leaves the old roadbed and begins climbing steeply into the Terror Creek drainage.
waypoints.directions: Continue up the old roadbed along Goodell Creek to roughly 4 miles, where a stone cairn marks the boot path leaving the roadbed to climb steeply into the Terror Creek drainage.

waypoints.name: Terror Creek Basin Camp
waypoints.note: Established campsite below the Barrier, with views of The Barrier, Degenhardt, Pyramid and the McMillan Spires.
waypoints.directions: Climb the steep boot path up the Terror Creek drainage on faint tread through dense brush, including a Class 3 root-pull section at a cliff band, then break out onto heather and talus to the camp at treeline in Terror Basin.

waypoints.name: The Barrier
waypoints.note: Steep, loose grassy ledge near 6,100 ft leading to serious class-3 scrambling on rotten rock to gain the crest around 6,400 ft.
waypoints.directions: From camp, climb west toward the Barrier, the steep headwall of the basin: a loose, grassy ledge near 6,100 ft leads to class 3 scrambling on rotten rock up to the crossing notch.

waypoints.name: Crescent Creek Basin High Camp
waypoints.note: High camp on the south side of Mount Terror, reached via an easy snow-ramp descent off the Barrier notch; also where enchainment parties arrive via the Otto-Himmel col.
waypoints.directions: Cross the notch and descend the easy snow ramp on the far side into Crescent Creek Basin, then contour north to the high camp on the south side of Mount Terror.

waypoints.name: Rubble Gully to the Terror-Rake Col
waypoints.note: Loose, rubble-choked gully leads to the notch between Mount Terror and The Rake; stay right on slightly harder class-3 rock to dodge the worst debris.
waypoints.directions: From camp, head north up to the deep, rubble-choked gully that leads to the notch between Mount Terror and The Rake, and climb it staying right on slightly harder but far more solid class 3 rock rather than in the debris of its bed.

waypoints.name: The Rake
waypoints.directions: Finish the gully to the Terror-Rake notch. The ridge starts immediately above on very steep rock with old fixed pins; follow roughly half a mile of serrated crest, mixed 4th and 5th class up to 5.9, to the summit.

waypoints.name: Stuart Lake Trailhead (end of FR 7601)
waypoints.directions: From US 2 at the west edge of Leavenworth, turn onto Icicle Creek Road and drive about 8.4 miles, then turn left onto Eightmile Road (Forest Road 7601) and follow the bumpy, potholed dirt road about 3.7 miles to the Stuart Lake Trailhead at road's end, about 3,400 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park, plus a free self-issued wilderness permit for a day trip.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Lake (outlet / north dam crossing)
waypoints.directions: Follow the Stuart Lake Trail #1599, crossing Mountaineer Creek on a log bridge near 1.5 miles, to the junction where the Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A forks left. Take it across a second Mountaineer Creek crossing and up steepening, rocky switchbacks to the north end of Colchuck Lake, about 4 miles and 2,280 ft from the trailhead.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Balanced Rock summit block
waypoints.directions: Cross the outlet below the small dam at the lake's north end and follow the climbers' path up and across the timbered hillside into the west cirque, then boulder-hop talus to the wall. The Scoop starts right of the West Face and the Tempest, left of Rikki Tikki Tavi; climb three pitches to Launch Ledge, the Scoop corner above it, and on to the summit block.

waypoints.name: Stuart Lake Trailhead (end of FR 7601)
waypoints.directions: From US 2 at the west end of Leavenworth, turn onto Icicle Road and follow it about 8.5 miles to the Bridge Creek Campground turnoff. Turn left onto FS Road 7601 and drive about 4 miles to its end at the Stuart Lake Trailhead, about 3,400 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or the day-use fee and a self-issued Enchantments day-use permit are required; FS Road 7601 is closed in winter, usually November to May.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Lake (outlet / north dam crossing)
waypoints.directions: Follow Stuart Lake Trail #1599 up the Mountaineer Creek valley, crossing the creek on a log bridge at about 1.5 miles. At the signed junction at about 2.5 miles fork left onto Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A, then switchback up a boulder moraine to the outlet of Colchuck Lake at about 4 miles and 5,570 ft. Fill water here; there is none higher.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Balanced Rock summit block
waypoints.directions: Follow the trail around the west shore of the lake to its south end and onto the cairned Aasgard Pass climbers' trail. Climb about 400 ft of talus and heather, then break climber's left through a dense band of slide alder and heather to the gully below the wall and scramble loose 3rd/4th class to the base. Climb the route's nine pitches to the summit block.

waypoints.name: Alpental / Snow Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Large gravel lot at the end of Alpental Road (1.5 mi past I-90 Exit 52); Northwest Forest Pass required to park.
waypoints.directions: Take I-90 to Exit 52 and follow Alpental Road to its end, about 1.5 miles, where a large gravel lot at roughly 3,100 ft serves as the trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park.

waypoints.name: Source Lake junction
waypoints.note: Signed spur splits toward the Source Lake overlook; leave the Snow Lake Trail here and head off-trail toward Great Scott Bowl for the South Face approach.
waypoints.directions: From the lot follow the Snow Lake Trail (#1013) north, climbing steadily through forest for about two miles and 1,000 ft to the small signed fork where the Source Lake spur splits off. Bear toward Source Lake. This is the last of the maintained tread — everything above it is off-trail.

waypoints.name: Great Scott Bowl talus/snow field
waypoints.note: Off-trail talus (snow-covered into early summer) beneath The Tooth's south side; loose rock and overhead rockfall risk from parties above, helmet recommended once you leave the trail.
waypoints.directions: Watch on the left as the trail curves for the point where a continuous talus field starts running alongside it, and leave the tread there. Traverse west into the boulders, losing a little height at first, then climb back up toward The Tooth's obvious south-facing wall by whatever line through talus and lingering snow gives least resistance. Helmets go on here: the bowl is loose and parties above will knock rock down it.

waypoints.name: Notch south of Pineapple Pass
waypoints.note: Gain this notch on the ridge just south of the true pass, then contour clockwise (exposed sidewalk traverse) to reach Pineapple Pass proper.
waypoints.directions: Work up the bowl aiming for the gully just left (south) of the prominent pointed rock partway up, and take that to the second notch south of the south face rather than trying to gain the pass directly. Early in the season this is a sustained steep snow climb that warrants an axe and sometimes crampons. A moat where the snow has pulled back from the rock often guards the last step onto the crest.

waypoints.name: Pineapple Pass
waypoints.note: Named saddle where pitch 1 of the South Face begins; a moat where seasonal snow pulls away from the rock can make the final step onto the col tricky into midsummer.
waypoints.directions: From the notch drop a short way down the far side, contour clockwise around beneath The Tooth, and climb back up to the pass. It is Class 3 to 4 but short and not exposed. The col is where the first pitch starts, so this is the place to rope up and sort the rack.

waypoints.name: The Catwalk
waypoints.note: Narrow, exposed rock traverse near the top of pitch 4 — the real crux of the climb despite the 5.4 rating; stay roped and protect it well.
waypoints.directions: Four short pitches of low fifth-class lead up from the pass: a groove trending right on juggy rock, connecting ledges past a pair of trees, an easy fourth-class ramble, then the steeper headwall. The Catwalk is the left-hand finish of that last pitch — a narrow, balancy ledge with a great deal of air beneath it. Two easier finishes exist to the right, and a steeper crack further left for parties wanting harder climbing.

waypoints.name: The Tooth summit
waypoints.note: Small, exposed summit block with views of Chair Peak, Bryant Peak and the Alpental valley; begin the four-rappel descent back to Pineapple Pass from anchors here.
waypoints.directions: From the end of the Catwalk a few metres of unroped scrambling tops out on the small summit block. There is no continuation off the far side — everyone comes back down the face they climbed — so keep the party gathered and organised for the rappels rather than spread across the top.

waypoints.name: Mineral Creek Trailhead (Trail #1331)
waypoints.note: Signed trailhead at the bottom of the valley on FR 4600, ~3 mi past Cooper Pass; self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk, no fee.
waypoints.directions: Drive FR-4600 over Cooper Pass and stay on it about 3 miles past the pass, down to the signed Mineral Creek Trailhead on the valley floor at roughly 2,360-2,400 ft. There is a self-issue wilderness permit kiosk at the trailhead and no fee, so fill one out before you start. Trail #1331 leaves the parking area and crosses the Kachess River almost immediately — look for logs spanning it, and expect a short, easy wade when they are not in place.

waypoints.name: Kachess River crossing
waypoints.note: Ford or rock-hop the Kachess River right at the start of the trail; can run thigh-deep in early-season high water.

waypoints.name: Old mine / end of mining-road tread
waypoints.note: Trail follows an old mining road through old-growth forest to this point, then narrows just before the wilderness boundary.

waypoints.name: Mineral Creek log crossing
waypoints.note: Cross Mineral Creek on a skinny, wet log (a crisscrossed pair aids balance); slick and exposed enough that some parties build/adjust a log bridge here.

waypoints.name: Leave Mineral Creek Trail for brush/gully ascent
waypoints.note: About a mile past the creek crossing, below the Three Queens massif, leave the maintained trail and start climbing brush and gully terrain toward open talus.

waypoints.name: Talus slope to the southeast shoulder
waypoints.note: Open talus that steepens and turns smaller and looser higher up leads to the broad southeast shoulder; loose underfoot.

waypoints.name: Traverse onto the northeast ridge
waypoints.note: Cross about a quarter mile of steep snow or talus from the shoulder to the northeast ridge; the step onto the ridge is the loosest, most exposed move of the day.

waypoints.name: Three Queens summit
waypoints.note: True summit, reached by the final loose, exposed stretch of the northeast ridge; test every hold.

removed.wp: Old mine / end of mining-road tread
Leave Mineral Creek Trail for brush/gully ascent

waypoints.name: Unsigned climbers' path off FS Road 56
waypoints.note: Faint, unsigned miners'/fishermen's path on the north side of Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road (FS 56), about 1.1 mi before the Dingford Creek Trailhead — easy to drive past.
waypoints.directions: From North Bend take I-90 exit 34 and follow 468th Ave SE north about 0.6 mile to the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road (FS Road 56). Continue roughly 16 miles up FS 56, which bends right around the 12-mile mark; the upper miles are rough gravel and dirt, and high clearance is recommended. You are aiming for an unsigned, easy-to-miss climbers' and fishermen's path on the north shoulder of the road at about 1,350 ft, roughly 1.1 miles before the Dingford Creek Trailhead. There is no sign and no formal parking area, so pull off where space allows.

waypoints.name: Green Ridge Lake trail fork
waypoints.note: Trail forks here; the right branch drops northeast to Green Ridge Lake, but the Treen Peak line stays left and continues steeply up the ridge.
waypoints.directions: Climb the steep, unmaintained miners' path straight up the forested flank of Green Ridge to the point where the trail forks.

waypoints.name: Point 4,840' ridge crest
waypoints.note: Ridge high point with panoramic views in all directions; leave the ridge trail here and go cross-country northwest toward Lake 4662.
waypoints.directions: Stay left where the right-hand branch drops northeast toward Green Ridge Lake, and keep climbing steeply up the ridge to its high point near 4,840 ft.

waypoints.name: Lake 4662 (tarn)
waypoints.note: Snowy tarn with Treen Peak framed dead ahead; useful early-season water source and the pivot point for dropping west into the Garfield lakes basin.
waypoints.directions: Leave the ridge trail at the high point and go cross-country a short way north to the small tarn, with Treen Peak in view ahead.

waypoints.name: Upper Garfield Mountain Lake
waypoints.note: Large lake at the head of the basin, about 800 ft below Point 4840 after the descent; informal shoreline campsites make this the usual overnight base.
waypoints.directions: From the tarn, descend north about 800 ft into the basin to the shore of Upper Garfield Mountain Lake. This drop has to be re-climbed on the way out.

waypoints.name: Charlie Brown Lake
waypoints.note: Reached via steep forest climb north from Upper Garfield Mountain Lake; from its outlet the route contours below Treen's gendarme-studded SW ridge.
waypoints.directions: Climb north from Upper Garfield Mountain Lake through steep forest to Charlie Brown Lake.

waypoints.name: Snow gully below the south-ridge notch
waypoints.note: Steep snow gully walled by rock on both sides directly north of Charlie Brown Lake, topping out at a notch by a protruding rock on the south ridge — carry an ice axe/crampons if snow lingers into summer.
waypoints.directions: From the outlet, work onto the peak's southeast slopes and thread up through broken cliff bands and loose duff to a broad talus field near 4,850 ft. From the top of the talus angle left into the obvious gully, walled by rock on both sides, and climb it to the notch beside a protruding rock on the south ridge. Carry an axe and traction if snow lingers.

waypoints.name: Treen Peak summit
waypoints.note: Elongated, corniced (north side) summit ridge with 360-degree views over the Middle Fork and Taylor River drainages and the Garfield lakes basin below.
waypoints.directions: Above the notch, climb a few hundred feet of easy but steep heather to the summit ridge and follow it to the top. The north side of the ridge is corniced.

waypoints.name: Smithbrook Trailhead
waypoints.note: Small dirt lot (~15 cars) off FR 6700; no parking pass required, no potable water or restrooms.
waypoints.directions: Drive US 2 to the Smithbrook Road turnoff, Forest Road 6700, about 4.2 miles east of the Stevens Pass summit — roughly half a mile east of milepost 69 if you are coming from the Leavenworth and Wenatchee side, or about 68 miles out from Everett and Seattle. Follow FR 6700 about 2.7 to 3 miles to the Smithbrook Trailhead at around 4,000 feet, on the left. The gravel road is normally passable to passenger cars once it is snow-free, but it is not plowed in winter; then you park at a pullout on the highway shoulder and add miles of road travel each way. The trailhead is a small dirt lot for about 15 cars, with no potable water and no restrooms.

waypoints.name: Rainy Creek tributary crossing
waypoints.note: Only reliable stream on this route — top off here, nothing higher on the ridge.
waypoints.directions: Start up Smithbrook Trail #1590 from the lot; a tributary of Rainy Creek crosses the trail about 0.2 mile in. It is the only reliable water on the route, so fill up here.

waypoints.name: Union Gap - PCT junction
waypoints.note: Smithbrook Trail #1590 switchbacks up old growth to this saddle and ends at the PCT; leave the maintained trail here for the boot path.
waypoints.directions: Continue up the trail as it switchbacks through old growth, about a mile from the trailhead, to the saddle at Union Gap, where it ends at the Pacific Crest Trail.

waypoints.name: Boulder field below the SE ridge
waypoints.note: First left off the PCT at a ~10-ft dead snag; boulder field lies to the north — follow cairns lined up with the snag to the field's high point.
waypoints.directions: Walk north on the PCT a short distance and take the first path breaking left off it at a standing dead snag about 10 ft tall. Follow the line of cairns set out from the snag north to the high point of the boulder field.

waypoints.name: SE ridge avalanche slope
waypoints.note: Steep, brush-choked slope gains the southeast ridge; brush is very slick when wet or snow-covered and this line is avalanche-prone on all aspects — not recommended in unstable snow.
waypoints.directions: From the top of the boulder field, climb the steep, brush-choked slope to gain the southeast ridge at about 5,200 ft. The brush is very slick when wet, and the slope is avalanche-prone in snow.

waypoints.name: Union Peak summit
waypoints.note: True summit, no maintained trail; open views down the Rainy Creek valley and along the PCT corridor toward Grizzly Peak.
waypoints.directions: Follow the southeast ridge crest northwest to the summit; the line is obvious once on the crest.

waypoints.name: Upper Dungeness Trailhead
waypoints.note: Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass required ($5/day, cashless payment only); trail #833.2 starts here into Buckhorn Wilderness.
waypoints.directions: From US-101 near Sequim Bay State Park, turn onto Louella Road and follow it for about a mile, then turn left onto Palo Alto Road for about 5.8 miles, where it has become FS Road 28 past the national forest boundary. Turn right onto FS Road 2880, pass Dungeness Forks Campground after about a mile, then stay left onto FS Road 2870 and follow it 8.7 miles to the Upper Dungeness Trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required at the kiosk, paid at $5/day, cashless only.

waypoints.name: Camp Handy
waypoints.note: Riverfront meadow with a cedar-shingle shelter along the Dungeness River; popular first-night camp and last easy water before the climb steepens.
waypoints.directions: Follow the Upper Dungeness Trail #833.2 upstream along the Dungeness River, staying left at the Royal Basin Trail junction, about 3.4 miles and 600 ft of gain to Camp Handy.

waypoints.name: Boulder Shelter
waypoints.note: Shelter structure amid large boulders after a steep 1,800+ ft climb from Camp Handy; the creek here is the most reliable water source before Home Lake.
waypoints.directions: Just past Camp Handy take the uphill fork and climb steeply, with two creek crossings, about 3 miles and 1,850 ft to Boulder Shelter.

waypoints.name: Home Lake
waypoints.note: Small alpine lake walled in by Mt. Constance and Warrior Peak; standard base camp for the climb, sits just below Constance Pass. Olympic NP wilderness permit (Recreation.gov) required.
waypoints.directions: From Boulder Shelter take the Constance Pass trail south rather than the trail toward Marmot Pass, cross into Olympic National Park, and continue past several creek crossings to Home Lake below Constance Pass.

waypoints.name: Warrior/Inner Constance cirque entry
waypoints.note: Leave the Home Lake basin and climb east into the Warrior/Inner Constance cirque through meadow and talus.
waypoints.directions: Leave the trail at Home Lake and climb east into the Warrior/Inner Constance cirque over meadow and talus to about 5,800 ft, where the headwall closes around the basin.

waypoints.name: Saddle couloir (rockfall/loose rock)
waypoints.note: Prominent north-northeast-trending couloir to the ~7,000 ft saddle between the twin summits; snow-filled and icy early season, a loose scree slog when melted out, with rockfall risk in the gully between the two peaks.
waypoints.directions: From the cirque head north into the obvious couloir that runs up between the twin summits, and climb it to the saddle at about 7,000 ft: snow early in the season, loose scree once it melts out. Watch for rockfall in the gully.

waypoints.name: Summit block rock step
waypoints.note: Above the saddle, 20-50 ft of exposed, poor-quality rock rated Class 4 to low 5th (5.2); many parties fix a hand line here for less-experienced climbers.
waypoints.directions: At the saddle turn right toward the higher southeast summit and cross to the foot of the summit block, where 20 to 50 ft of exposed, poor rock on its northwest side is the crux, often reached over steep snow or a moat.

waypoints.name: Warrior Peak (Southeast Summit)
waypoints.note: True summit is the southeast of the two tied peaks (~7,320 ft); Fred Beckey made the first ascent of both summits solo in 1945.
waypoints.directions: Climb the Class 4 to low 5th rock step, roped or on a fixed hand line if needed, and scramble the last short distance to the southeast summit.
